prompt: Some friends are having a conversation about how boring things have gotten ... in the middle of a comically dramatic / dangerous / or otherwise intense scene .
content:
### The Most Interesting Tuesday

“I’m just saying,” said Mina, gripping the wooden ribs of the dragon’s neck, “life has gotten boring.”

The dragon lurched sideways.

Outside, the parade crowd gasped as the enormous papier-mâché beast rolled down Main Street at a speed not usually associated with papier-mâché. Its painted eyes bulged. Its cardboard wings flapped in the wind. Beneath its belly, four friends clung to a bench bolted onto the float’s trailer.

“Boring?” cried Theo. “We are currently inside a dragon that has escaped its parade.”

“Exactly,” Mina said. “This is the most interesting Tuesday we’ve had in months.”

“It’s Saturday,” said Ben.

“That’s how boring things have gotten. I’ve lost track of the days.”

A gust shoved the dragon forward. The float’s little wheels bounced over a pothole. Somewhere overhead, a papier-mâché claw ripped loose and sailed into the crowd. The crowd cheered, apparently assuming it was part of the show.

At the front of the bench, Ravi wrestled with the steering wheel, which had been installed for decoration and was not connected to anything.

“Can we focus on stopping?” he yelled.

“We are focused,” said Ben. “We’re discussing why we failed to stop sooner.”

The float gathered speed down the hill toward the town square. At the bottom stood a fountain, a bandstand, and a row of booths selling lemonade. Beyond those was the river.

Mina looked at the river. “I’d like to amend my complaint. Life has gotten too interesting.”

“Noted,” said Ben. “I’ll put it in the minutes.”

The dragon’s tail whipped behind them, knocking over a banner that read **WELCOME, HISTORICAL SOCIETY!** The banner wrapped around a lamppost. For one glorious second, it slowed the float.

Then it snapped.

The dragon shot forward.

Ravi grabbed a cord hanging from the ceiling. “What’s this?”

“Probably decorative,” said Mina.

He pulled it.

The dragon’s head dropped over the front of the float, blocking their view.

“Good news,” Ravi shouted. “We have successfully made it harder to see where we’re going!”

Ben leaned toward the dragon’s side and peered through a gap in the cardboard scales. “Fountain in thirty seconds!”

“Can we steer?” Mina asked.

“Not with the steering wheel,” said Ravi.

“Can we brake?”

“Not with the brakes.”

“Can we jump?”

“Not at this speed!”

“Then I would like to return to discussing my original point.”

The float thundered past the lemonade booths. A vendor threw a stack of napkins at them. The napkins fluttered through the dragon like tiny surrender flags.

Mina caught one and held it up. “See? People are finally paying attention to us.”

“We wanted attention?” Ben yelled.

“I wanted someone to ask how my pottery class was going!”

“I asked!”

“You said, ‘Is that the one with the mud?’”

“It is the one with the mud!”

Ahead, the fountain rose in the sunlight. A team of volunteers had piled hay bales beside it for the parade’s finale. The bales were meant to cushion a tumbling acrobat. Nobody had expected to cushion a dragon.

“Hay!” shouted Ravi.

“Wonderful,” said Mina. “I’ve always wanted to be saved by agricultural leftovers.”

The dragon bounced over the curb, clipped the edge of the bandstand, and spun. The four friends grabbed each other as the world became a blur of painted scales, blue sky, and one very startled town mayor.

Then—*whump*.

The float plunged into the hay bales. Straw burst everywhere. The dragon’s head popped off and rolled gently into the fountain, where it floated like a very confused duck.

For a moment, nobody moved.

Then Ben brushed straw from his hair. “So. Same time next Saturday?”

Mina looked at the dragon’s head, bobbing in the fountain. “Only if we do something exciting.”

Ravi climbed out of the wreckage. “I’m going to suggest pottery.”

“Is it the one with the mud?” Ben asked.

Mina sighed. “Life has gotten boring again already.”

prompt: The time of Armageddon is soon . All the gods of various pantheons congregate to debate on why their end of the world should happen . While squabbling among each other , a god that was never worshiped speaks its mind .
content:
## The God No One Prayed To

Armageddon was scheduled for Thursday.

The gods had gathered outside time, in a hall built from the bones of dead stars. There were thunder-kings and river mothers, sun-bright queens and pale lords of the underworld. There were gods with names spoken in a million temples, and gods whose names had survived only in the oldest songs.

At the center of the hall stood a long table. Above it turned a little blue world, its oceans shining.

“Mine is the proper ending,” declared the Thunder-King, and lightning crawled over his knuckles. “A final storm. The mountains split. The proud are humbled.”

“You have already tried that,” said the River Mother. “Your flood drowned the innocent along with the proud.”

“That is the trouble with floods,” he grumbled. “They’re difficult to aim.”

The Red Judge leaned over the table. “Let the dead rise. Let every forgotten wrong be weighed. The world should end beneath the burden of its own cruelty.”

A Sun Queen tilted her golden head. “Dramatic, but wasteful. I would burn the sky clean. One perfect dawn, and then nothing.”

Around the table, the other gods offered their endings: a final winter, a devouring serpent, a great silence, a door opening in the earth. Each spoke of justice. Each spoke of necessity. Each glanced at the others to see who was impressed.

The little blue world turned beneath them.

“You are all missing the point,” said the One-Eyed Wanderer. “The end should be a test. Only those with courage—”

“Oh, do be quiet,” said the River Mother. “You’ve made every age a test.”

The table shuddered. A crack appeared in the blue world, a thin glowing seam from pole to pole.

Beyond the hall, time began to run faster.

Thursday was coming.

Then a voice spoke from the doorway.

“I think you should end.”

The gods fell silent.

In the doorway stood a small, plainly dressed figure. No crown, no spear, no halo. The figure might have been old or young. It was hard to tell. Their face had the familiar quality of someone you had seen in a dream and forgotten by breakfast.

The Thunder-King frowned. “Who are you?”

“I have many names,” said the figure. “None of them lasted.”

The gods looked at one another.

The Red Judge searched the figure’s face for a mark of divinity. The Sun Queen looked for a constellation. The One-Eyed Wanderer peered with his remaining eye.

At last the River Mother asked, “What do you rule?”

“Nothing.”

“Then why are you here?”

“Because I have been listening.”

A few gods laughed. The sound was uncertain.

The figure stepped toward the table. “I am the god of what people do when they think no god is watching. A hand held out. A meal divided. A truth told when a lie would be easier.”

The laughter stopped.

“I have never had a temple,” the figure continued. “No one has prayed to me. People call those things kindness, or luck, or simply what you do. They don’t ask me to make them happen. They just do them.”

The Sun Queen’s light dimmed a fraction. “And you think that qualifies you to judge us?”

“No,” said the figure. “I think it qualifies me to recognize you.”

They looked around the table, at the gods who had shaped mountains and commanded seas, who had been feared and adored and begged for mercy.

“You are arguing over which of you gets to destroy the world,” the figure said. “But none of you wants the world to end. You want to be the one who ends it.”

The thunder in the Thunder-King’s hands faded.

“You want the last word,” the figure said. “You want the world to look up, at the final moment, and know it was yours.”

The crack across the little blue world widened. Its oceans trembled. Far below, a city’s lights flickered as the hour approached.

The Red Judge rose. “If we do nothing, what becomes of us?”

The figure glanced at the turning world. “The same thing that becomes of every ruler when the people stop asking permission.”

The gods looked down.

There were no prayers rising from the cities now. Not because people had ceased believing, but because they were busy. A nurse steadied a patient’s hand. A boy held an umbrella over a stranger. A woman carried soup upstairs to an old neighbor. In a dozen places, people reached for one another without asking heaven to approve.

The One-Eyed Wanderer lowered his staff. “So this is the ending?”

“No,” said the figure. “This is the part where you decide what ends.”

For a long time, none of the gods spoke.

Then the River Mother placed both hands on the table. “Let the age of our rule end.”

The Thunder-King looked at the world, where storm clouds had begun to gather. He closed his fist. The clouds passed.

One by one, the gods withdrew their endings. The serpent curled into sleep. The dead returned to their graves. Winter loosened its hold. The sun kept its fire, but softened it to morning.

At last, only the little figure remained beside the table.

“What will they call you?” asked the Sun Queen.

The figure considered this.

“Probably nothing,” they said.

Thursday came.

The world did not end.

And that morning, in a city beneath a clearing sky, a stranger shared an umbrella with a woman carrying a bowl of soup. Neither of them looked up. Neither of them thought to give thanks.

The god at the doorway smiled. It was enough.

prompt: Special Division Infantry , Necromancer Class .
content:
### The Necromancer’s Division

The Special Division Infantry had three rules.

Never remove your helmet inside the dead zone.

Never answer a voice that called from beneath the ground.

And never, under any circumstances, let the Necromancer Class lead.

Captain Mara Venn had broken all three before sunrise.

Her helmet lay cracked in the mud beside her. The voice beneath the ground had called her by her childhood nickname. And she was at the front of the column, walking toward the ruined city of Bellweather with a lantern in one hand and a company of the dead behind her.

“Captain,” Sergeant Hales whispered over the radio. “The map says the eastern road is clear.”

“The map is wrong.”

“Respectfully, ma’am, the map was made yesterday.”

“Then it’s a very fresh mistake.”

Ahead, Bellweather’s rooftops leaned together beneath a sky the color of old iron. No birds circled the towers. No smoke rose from chimneys. The city had been empty for six years—empty of the living, at least.

Mara lifted her lantern.

Its blue flame bent toward the ground.

“Positions,” she said.

The infantry spread out. Their armor was gray, their rifles silver-edged, their faces hidden behind masks. They had been trained to fight anything that moved. Mara’s training had been different. She had learned how to speak to things that didn’t.

A hand broke through the road.

Then another.

The soldiers raised their rifles.

“Hold,” Mara ordered.

More hands emerged. Pale fingers gripped the stones as bodies dragged themselves out of the earth. Uniforms. Old rifles. Familiar shoulder patches.

The dead of the First Bellweather Company.

A young private made a strangled sound. “They’re coming for us.”

“No,” Mara said. “They’re coming to attention.”

She stepped forward and removed her gloves. The cold bit into her fingers.

“Sergeant,” she said, “tell them we’ve come to relieve them.”

Hales stared. “I don’t speak dead.”

“Neither do they. Not anymore.”

Mara pressed her palm against the nearest corpse’s brow.

The world opened.

She felt six years of darkness—the weight of the buried city, the last desperate minutes of the old company, the terrible thing that had taken Bellweather and left its victims unable to rest. The dead had not risen because they were hungry. They had risen because someone had finally called them by their names.

Mara closed her eyes.

“Private Doss,” she said. “Corporal Ilyan. Sergeant Vale. Lieutenant Orro.”

One by one, the dead lowered their weapons.

Behind her, the living infantry lowered theirs too.

Then the city bells began to ring.

Every window filled with a shadow.

Something vast moved beneath the streets, pushing up the cobbles in a long, slow wave. The old company turned as one toward the sound. Their empty eyes fixed on Mara.

The voice from beneath the ground spoke again.

*Little Wren.*

Mara’s throat tightened.

Her mother had called her that. Her mother, who had died in Bellweather while Mara was still a child.

The dead shifted uneasily. The thing below them had learned the voice from their memories.

“Captain,” Hales said. “We need to fall back.”

Mara looked at the city. At the shadows in the windows. At the soldiers who had been waiting six years for someone to give them an order.

“No,” she said. “We need to finish the fight.”

She turned to the dead company.

“First Bellweather,” she called. “You are relieved.”

For a heartbeat, nothing happened.

Then Sergeant Vale raised his rusted rifle.

“About time,” he said.

The dead charged.

The living followed.

Mara ran between them, lantern blazing blue in the gray morning. The bells rang harder. The road split open. And beneath Bellweather, the thing that had been feeding on the city’s silence woke at last to the sound of an army marching toward it.

prompt: Write a good fight scene .
content:
The bell began to ring as the river reached the first stair.

Mara was halfway across the old footbridge when Captain Venn stepped from the fog, sword drawn. Behind him, the town’s last ferry strained at its ropes, crowded with people. One cut, and the current would take it.

“You’re late,” Venn said.

“I was helping them leave.”

“You were helping them run.”

He swung.

Mara caught the blow on her saber. The impact rattled her arm to the shoulder. She shoved him back, but Venn had already turned the force aside; his boot swept for her knee. She hopped over it, landed badly on the slick planks, and barely got her blade up before his next strike.

They had trained together for twelve years. Venn knew every feint she knew, every opening she favored. He had taught her to watch an opponent’s shoulders.

So Mara watched his feet.

When he stepped in, she didn’t block. She slipped sideways and drove her elbow into his ribs. Venn grunted, stumbled into the bridge rail, and nearly went over. Mara lunged for his sword hand.

He head-butted her.

White light burst behind her eyes. She staggered, tasting blood, and Venn tore free. His blade flashed down. Mara caught it against the crossguard of her saber, their faces inches apart.

“Still too slow,” he growled.

“Still talking too much.”

She stamped on his instep.

Venn’s grip loosened. Mara twisted, but he let go of his sword before she could wrench it away and punched her hard in the stomach. The air left her. She folded; he seized her collar and hurled her against the railing.

The old bridge shuddered. One of its support ropes snapped with a sound like a gunshot.

Across the gap, someone screamed.

Mara looked toward the ferry. Its ropes were fraying, the boat already swinging into the current. There was no time to beat Venn properly. There was only time to stop him.

She seized the loose support rope and wrapped it around her forearm.

Venn glanced at it. “You’ll pull the bridge down.”

“Maybe.”

He came at her.

Mara ducked beneath his first slash and drove her shoulder into his chest. They hit the boards together. His sword skittered away. Venn landed on top, fist raised, but Mara caught his wrist with both hands.

For a moment they strained, neither moving. Rain ran down Venn’s face. He looked older than she remembered.

“The town needs order,” he said.

“It needs people.”

She turned her hips and rolled. Venn hit the planks beside her. Mara scrambled up, but he caught her ankle and dragged her down again. His hand closed around her throat.

The bridge lurched.

The support rope burned through Mara’s sleeve. She let go with one hand, reached for the fallen sword, and struck the planks between them. The blade punched through the wood. Venn flinched at the sudden splintering crack.

Mara drove her forehead into his nose and shoved him away.

He rolled to the edge. She reached for him without thinking.

Venn caught her wrist.

For a breath, they hung together over the black water: his grip on her, hers on him, the bridge groaning beneath them.

“Let go,” he said.

Mara tightened her hold. “Not this time.”

She hauled him back onto the boards.

Behind them, the ferry’s last rope gave way. The boat swung free, carried by the river—but pointed downstream, toward the open channel.

Venn stared after it. His sword lay between them.

Mara stood, breathing hard. “You can come with us.”

He looked at the ferry, then at her. At last, he lowered his empty hands.

The bell rang once more above them, and the bridge held.

prompt: Death comes to collect someone and ends up falling in love with them .
content:
**The Last Light**

Death arrived at the lighthouse at eleven fifty-seven on a night of hard rain.

He had expected the door to be locked. It was, but the old woman inside opened it before he could knock.

“You’re late,” she said.

Death glanced at the watch he wore out of habit. “I’m three minutes early.”

“Then you’re early. Either way, I’ve put the kettle on.”

Her name was Mara Vale. She had kept the lighthouse for forty-two years, first with her husband, then alone. Now the beam turned above them, sweeping its pale circle over the black sea.

Death stepped inside and shut the door against the weather. His coat didn’t drip. It never did.

Mara looked him up and down. “I thought you’d be taller.”

“I’m sorry to disappoint you.”

“I’m not. Tall people are always bumping their heads.”

She led him into the kitchen. On the table sat two cups and a plate of buttered toast.

“You can eat?” she asked.

“No.”

“Can you smell?”

“No.”

“Can you at least pretend to enjoy the tea?”

“I can try.”

“Good. I’ve spent a lifetime making tea for people who didn’t deserve it. I’d hate to stop now.”

Death sat. Mara poured. Her hands trembled a little, but the stream landed neatly in both cups.

For a while, they listened to the rain worrying at the windows.

“You know why I’m here,” he said.

“I know.”

“Are you afraid?”

Mara considered this. “Yes. But not of you.”

“What are you afraid of?”

“That I’ll leave the light on too long.”

Death looked toward the staircase, where the turning beam passed and passed again, brightening the room for an instant. “Someone will take over.”

“Someone always does.” She smiled faintly. “That doesn’t mean I have to like it.”

He had heard many answers to his question. Most people asked for more time. Some bargained. Some cursed him. A few welcomed him as though they’d been waiting at a station.

No one had ever worried about a lamp.

Mara pushed the plate toward him. “Have a piece.”

“I can’t.”

“You’re very difficult to host.”

“I’m often told that.”

She laughed, and the sound filled the kitchen more warmly than the stove.

They talked while the storm battered the island. Mara told him about her husband, who had been a terrible cook and an excellent whistler. She told him about the ship that had gone aground in a fog so thick the lighthouse beam looked like a solid wall. She told him about a gull that stole her keys and dropped them into the sea.

Death listened. He had carried away kings and children, sailors and strangers. He knew the facts of countless lives. But Mara spoke of hers as if it were a place he might visit: the warmth of a hand around a chipped mug, the smell of wet wool, the particular hush that came just before dawn.

At twelve thirty, she showed him the keeper’s room. At one, she showed him the narrow stair to the lantern. At two, she found a deck of cards and taught him a game.

He won every hand.

“You’re cheating,” she said.

“I don’t know how to cheat.”

“You know everything that’s about to happen.”

“Not everything.”

“Then let me win one.”

He tried. She saw through it and scolded him anyway.

By three, the storm had softened to rain. They sat beneath the lantern, watching the beam travel out over the water. Mara’s breathing had grown shallow. The pauses between her words were longer now.

Death stood. “It’s time.”

Mara looked at him. “I know.”

He held out his hand. It was pale and perfectly still.

She didn’t take it at once. “What happens when we go?”

“I take you where you need to go.”

“And you?”

“I return.”

“To the next person?”

“Yes.”

“Alone?”

Death had no answer.

Mara reached for his hand. Her fingers were warm. His were not, but he felt the shape of her touch as if it were the first thing he had ever been given.

“I’m sorry,” she said.

“For what?”

“For you having to do this alone.”

He looked at her then—not at her fading breath, not at the appointed hour, but at the woman who had offered him tea, and toast he could not eat, and a card game she knew he would win. Something in him opened, though he had no heart to name it.

“I don’t want to lose you,” he said.

Mara’s expression softened. “You don’t have to want it.”

“Can I come with you?”

“Where I’m going?”

“Yes.”

She squeezed his hand. “You’re already coming.”

The lighthouse beam crossed the room once more. When it passed, Mara was gone.

Death stood beneath the lantern, holding her empty cup.

Outside, the rain stopped. Dawn began to pale the horizon. The light kept turning, sweeping its bright circle over the sea, over the rocks, over the path that led down from the tower.

Death stayed until sunrise.

Then he went to collect the next soul—and, for the first time in all his long existence, he carried someone’s warmth with him.

prompt: Terrestrial humans , as depicted by beings on other planets .
content:
## The Terrestrials

In the Museum of Neighboring Worlds, the exhibit on Earth was always crowded.

Visitors drifted past the glass cases, pointing at the tiny blue planet turning beneath a dome of artificial stars. They studied the human artifacts arranged around it: a rusted key, a child’s red mitten, a chipped cup painted with flowers.

The museum’s official description read:

**TERRESTRIAL HUMANS**  
*An anxious, tool-making species. Known to divide their habitat into territories, then cross those territories to visit one another.*

Most visitors laughed at that last part.

Mara did not. She was the youngest curator on the museum’s staff, and she had spent three years listening to Earth’s old transmissions.

“They’re not just anxious,” she said to her supervisor, Oru. “They’re also curious.”

Oru’s pale fronds rippled with amusement. “Curiosity is what anxious creatures call their habit of touching things they don’t understand.”

Mara pointed toward the display. “Then why did they keep sending messages into the dark?”

The transmissions were old, most of them broken into static. The museum had gathered them from probes and drifting machines: voices traveling through space long after the people who made them had gone quiet.

A human child counted.

A human woman sang.

A human voice, hoarse with cold, called out coordinates while other voices answered. The recording ended with a burst of noise, then silence.

“They were describing themselves,” Mara said. “Not for us. For anyone.”

Oru folded his long hands. “A species that broadcasts its own existence is either very brave or very poor at estimating danger.”

“Maybe both.”

That evening, Mara stayed after closing and opened the exhibit’s oldest recording. It had been marked *Unverified Music*. A slow melody filled the hall, wavering and imperfect. Beneath it, someone spoke in a language the museum had only partly translated.

Mara read the caption aloud.

“‘This is for my daughter. If you hear it, I hope you’re safe.’”

The next morning, she changed the exhibit.

She removed the diagram of human weapons and replaced it with a map of Earth’s coastlines, marked with the names of cities that no longer existed. Beside it, she placed a recording of rain on a roof. Then a child laughing. Then a crowd, shouting together—not in anger, the translation assured her, but in celebration.

Oru inspected the new display.

“You’ve made them seem sentimental,” he said.

“They were sentimental.”

“Sentiment is not a complete description.”

“No,” Mara agreed. “Neither is ‘anxious tool-making species.’”

She added a final placard:

**THE TERRESTRIALS WERE SMALL, AND THEIR WORLD WAS NOT KIND TO THEM.**  
**THEY BUILT SHELTERS, STORIES, AND MACHINES TO REACH BEYOND IT.**  
**THEY OFTEN HURT ONE ANOTHER. THEY ALSO CARRIED ONE ANOTHER THROUGH FIRE, FLOOD, AND DARKNESS.**  
**WE DO NOT KNOW WHICH OF THESE THINGS THEY WOULD HAVE WANTED US TO REMEMBER.**

The museum opened at dawn.

Visitors paused before the exhibit. Some frowned at the new words. Some listened to the music. One young visitor pressed a hand to the glass, just above the little red mitten.

“What happened to them?” she asked.

Mara watched Earth turn slowly beneath its dome.

“We don’t know,” she said.

The child considered this. “Could they still be out there?”

Mara glanced at the star map, at all those distant suns, each with its own planets, its own storms, its own small lives looking up.

“Possibly,” she said. “And if they are, I hope someone is listening.”

{prompt}
prompt: For as long as you can remember , you can hear background music appropriate to the situation you 're in . While going to the grocery store one day , you hear what sounds like the most generic JRPG battle theme you 've ever heard .
content:
For as long as I can remember, there has been music.

Not music I can turn off. Not music anyone else can hear. Just a private soundtrack that follows me around: soft piano when I’m tired, bright little strings when I’m hopeful, dramatic brass when I’m running late and the bus is pulling away.

It’s usually right about the mood. It’s not always subtle.

On Tuesday, I went to the grocery store for coffee, eggs, and the special kind of cat food my cat will eat for exactly six days before deciding she hates it. I was halfway through the produce section when the music changed.

A drumbeat. A heroic brass fanfare. Then a chugging string melody that sounded as if it had been written by someone who had been told, “Make it adventurous, but we don’t have much time or budget.”

I stopped beside the avocados.

The tune looped.

It was, without question, the most generic JRPG battle theme I had ever heard. The sort of music that played while a party of four fought three slimes in a grassy field. A song that suggested danger, but not *important* danger.

I looked around. No monsters. No suspicious movement. Just a man comparing two kinds of hummus.

The music looped again.

I put the avocados back and followed the aisle toward the registers, because the soundtrack had never been wrong before. It had accompanied my first kiss with a gentle swell of strings, my worst haircut with a mournful oboe, and the time I dropped an entire lasagna on the kitchen floor with a single, plangent piano chord.

The battle music got louder near checkout.

At register four, a young man was counting coins into his palm. A carton of eggs, a loaf of bread, and a tin of formula sat on the belt. Behind him, a toddler in the shopping cart was chewing the corner of a receipt.

The cashier scanned the formula. The young man’s card declined.

“Sorry,” he said. He tapped it again, as if the machine might have changed its mind.

The machine had not.

He looked at the total, then at the formula. “Could you take this off?”

The cashier nodded and reached for the tin.

The battle music pounded in my ears.

I felt around in my pocket for my wallet. I had enough to cover it, probably. If I skipped coffee for a couple of days. Maybe bought the cheap cat food and dealt with the consequences. My cat would survive. She’d make sure I knew I’d let her down, but she’d survive.

Still, there was a little voice in my head saying: *Not your problem.*

There was a second voice, the one that had apparently been given a brass section, saying: *It is now.*

“I can get it,” I said.

The young man turned toward me. “No, I’m okay.”

“Are you sure? Because I’m already here, and this is the most exciting thing that’s happened to me all week.”

He gave a startled laugh. The cashier paused with the tin in her hand.

“I can pay you back,” he said.

“You don’t have to.” I slid my card into the machine. “Really. I once paid eighteen dollars for a salad that came with three almonds. This will make me feel like I’ve finally balanced the books.”

That got a proper smile.

The card went through. The cashier tucked the formula into the bag. The toddler, having lost interest in the receipt, reached for the tin and was gently redirected toward a banana.

The young man thanked me twice. Then he picked up the bags and headed for the door.

The battle music continued for three more beats, apparently waiting for a victory animation. Then it gave a bright little flourish and faded into the store’s ordinary Muzak.

I paid for my coffee, eggs, and the cat food.

Outside, the air was cold and clean. Somewhere inside the store, the young man’s toddler was probably making a run at the receipt again.

I started walking home. The music that replaced the battle theme was warm, simple piano.

It was a little generic, too.

But it fit.

content:
## The Most Beautiful Woman in the World

The first thing the museum did was put her on a billboard.

Her face, enlarged to the height of a building, looked down on the city with smooth cheeks and solemn eyes. Beneath it, in gold letters, ran the title the auction house had given the painting:

**THE MOST BEAUTIFUL WOMAN IN THE WORLD**

Ada Vale was less impressed. She was the museum’s paintings conservator, and she had spent twenty years looking closely at faces other people admired from a distance. This one had been varnished until it shone like honey. Someone had painted over the woman’s mouth, making it smaller, and softened the line of her jaw. The eyes had been nudged forward, toward the viewer.

“She’s been improved,” said Mr. Bell, the curator, surveying the portrait in its workroom.

“By whom?” Ada asked.

“By someone with very definite opinions.”

She leaned toward the canvas. Under the woman’s right eye, a tiny crescent of darker paint showed through the varnish. Not a shadow. A brushstroke.

“Someone changed her expression,” Ada said.

Mr. Bell sighed. “Please don’t tell the press she’s been tampered with until we know what that means.”

“I wasn’t going to tell the press anything.”

“Good. They’ve already booked three television crews for the unveiling.”

When he left, Ada switched on the infrared camera.

The painted-over face appeared on the monitor in ghostly lines. There was the original mouth: open, almost laughing. The original eyes were turned slightly to the left, toward something beyond the edge of the canvas. And there, where the later painter had perfected the woman’s skin, the first artist had left a faint smudge of blue.

Ada enlarged the image.

Ink, perhaps.

She returned to the museum’s archive after closing, searching for the painting’s history. It had passed through five collections and two wars before arriving at the auction house. For nearly a century it had been called *Portrait of a Lady*. The grand title appeared only in a catalogue from 1924.

At the bottom of a box of old correspondence, Ada found a letter from the painter, Tomas Venn, to his sister.

*I have painted the most beautiful woman in the world,* he wrote. *She would not sit still. She kept turning toward the courtyard because the little one was trying to walk. There is ink on her cuff, and she has laughed at me for noticing. I have tried to catch the moment before she gets up.*

The woman’s name, in a different hand, had been written in the margin: **Elian Venn.**

Ada sat very still.

The next morning she asked Mr. Bell to come look at the infrared images.

He stared at them. “So the famous portrait is a mother watching her child?”

“Apparently.”

“And the face was altered later?”

“Yes.”

“Can you put it back?”

“I can remove the later paint. I can’t promise what the original will look like. It’s fragile.”

He rubbed the bridge of his nose. “The billboard is already printed.”

Ada returned to the studio. “Then the billboard can be wrong for a few more weeks.”

For the next month, she worked beneath a magnifying lens, lifting the later paint a flake at a time. The woman gradually emerged—not younger, not prettier, but more present. Her mouth was caught between a smile and a word. Her eyes rested on something just outside the frame. The blue on her cuff proved to be ink.

On the day of the unveiling, the museum filled with people. Cameras waited. Mr. Bell stood beside Ada beneath a white cloth.

When he pulled it away, the crowd leaned forward.

For a moment, no one spoke. The face on the canvas wasn’t the face from the billboard. She seemed distracted, almost impatient. A loose curl fell across her forehead. Her gaze belonged to someone else.

Then a small girl near the front tugged at her father’s sleeve.

“She’s looking at somebody,” the girl whispered.

Her father followed the painted eyes. “Yes,” he said. “I think she is.”

The museum kept the title. The press insisted on it; titles, like varnish, are difficult to remove once they’ve dried. But beside the painting, the new label read:

**Elian Venn, by Tomas Venn, 1891.**  
**The painter described her as “the most beautiful woman in the world.”**

Years later, when Ada visited the gallery, she found a woman standing before the portrait with a sleeping child on her shoulder. The child’s blue mitten was smudged with ink.

The woman looked up at Elian, and Elian seemed to look back.

Ada smiled.

At last, the painting had its audience.

content:
### The Hearing

You wake beneath a portrait of Franz Kafka.

The room smells of wet wool and dust. Your wrists are tied to the arms of a wooden chair. On the table in front of you, beneath a glass dome, rests a copy of *The Trial*. Its spine has been repaired with black tape. Someone has underlined whole paragraphs in red.

A man sits opposite you, hands folded. He is thin, silver-haired, and dressed like a schoolteacher.

“Mr. Vale,” he says. “I’m the presiding officer.”

“You kidnapped me.”

“Your first statement is noted.”

He lifts the glass dome and takes out the book. “You know this story?”

“I read it in college.”

“Then you know what happens to Josef K.”

“I know he’s accused without being told why.”

“And eventually?”

“He’s killed.”

Vale nods, pleased. “Good. We won’t have to waste time explaining the sacred text.”

He says the book is not a novel. It is a record: an account of the law that governs every human life, disguised as fiction so people would accept it. The cult has spent years rebuilding the process described in its pages. There are hearings, clerks, informants, corridors that lead nowhere. There is a court in the old courthouse upstairs.

“And what happens to me?” you ask.

“You will be charged.”

“With what?”

“That will be revealed at the hearing.”

“When?”

“Tomorrow.”

“And after that?”

“If the text is followed correctly, you will be executed.”

The calmness in his voice is worse than a threat. You tug once at the ropes. They bite your wrists.

“Why tell me?”

Vale looks down at the book. “K. was never told what was happening to him. We are correcting that mistake.”

For a moment, you have nothing to say. Then: “You think the book tells you what to do.”

“I think it tells us what is already being done.”

They leave you in a cell beneath the courthouse. The room has a narrow window set too high to see through. At intervals, you hear footsteps overhead, then the murmur of people gathering.

In the morning, two guards bring you up.

The courtroom is a school auditorium. The judge’s bench is a lectern. On the wall behind it hangs another portrait of Kafka, this one larger, his painted eyes turned slightly toward the door. About thirty people sit in the audience. Some look frightened. Others look tired. A few stare at you as if they’re waiting for you to say something they’ve rehearsed.

Vale stands at the lectern.

“The accused will hear the charge.”

A clerk unfolds a paper. “The accused is charged with entering the jurisdiction of the Court without permission, and with refusing to recognize its authority.”

“How can I be charged for refusing to recognize something I wasn’t told existed?” you ask.

The clerk glances at Vale.

“Questions are not answers,” Vale says.

“Then what is the point of a hearing?”

A quiet stir passes through the audience. Vale’s expression doesn’t change, but he grips the lectern.

“The accused will be given time to consider the charge.”

They take you back downstairs.

That night, a young woman brings your supper. She sets the tray down and lingers by the door.

“What happens to people after the hearing?” you ask.

She looks at the ceiling, as if the room might be listening. “They tell us the ending is inevitable.”

“Do you believe that?”

“I used to.”

She leaves before you can ask anything else.

At the final hearing, Vale reads the sentence before the clerk has finished reading the charge. The audience sits silent. The young woman is there, near the back, her hands clenched in her lap.

Vale asks if you have anything to say.

“Yes,” you tell him. “The book is describing what happens when people surrender their judgment to a system they can’t question.”

He gives a tired smile. “That is what the accused always says.”

“Does the book say you should build this court?”

No one moves.

“Does it say you should kidnap people? Tie them up? Choose a stranger and call them guilty?”

Vale’s fingers tighten around the edge of the lectern. “The text requires a witness.”

“The text is paper.”

A murmur runs through the room. The young woman stands.

“I was told I was the next accused,” she says.

Vale turns toward her. “Sit down.”

“I was told there was no appeal.”

“There is no appeal.”

“Then why are we here?”

The silence changes. It is no longer the silence of a congregation. It is the silence of people waiting for someone else to answer first.

The young woman walks to the side door. A guard reaches for her, then stops. She turns the handle.

It opens.

Vale says your name—not the one you gave him, but the one on the papers they stole from your wallet. He says it like a verdict.

You step down from the platform.

For a moment, the room seems to hold its breath. Then you follow the young woman through the door. Behind you, Vale begins reading again, louder now, as if volume can make the words holy.

Outside, dawn is breaking over the courthouse steps.

The young woman doesn’t ask where you’re going. Neither do you. You walk toward the street, away from the locked doors, while behind you the hearing carries on without its accused.

prompt: In a world where simulations have become the norm , it gets increasingly difficult to tell the difference between simulation and reality . You 've just met the girl of your dreams , literally . Only thing is you ca n't tell if she 's real or a figment if the simulation .
content:
### The Shape of a Dream

By the time I met Lena, I had already dreamed her for three years.

Not every night. Dreams were less reliable than weather and more private than passwords. Still, she came back: dark hair tucked behind one ear, a small scar at her chin, a smile like she’d just remembered something funny about me.

I never knew her name. I only knew that in the dreams, we were always about to meet.

Then, on an ordinary Tuesday, she stepped out of a virtual bakery in the city sim and nearly walked into me.

The city was called Common Ground, though nobody called it that. We went there to shop, work, wander, and avoid the rain. Most people wore their own faces. Some preferred wings, or younger faces, or bodies they’d designed from scratch. The city adjusted to whatever your device could render, so even people with cheap rigs saw the same sunset.

Lena wore a green coat. She had the scar.

I stopped so abruptly that a cyclist passed through my shoulder.

She looked at me. “You okay?”

I stared.

Her smile appeared, a little crooked at one side.

“I know you,” I said.

She glanced around. “I don’t think so.”

“Sorry. I just—”

“Have we met in a dream?” she asked.

The words struck me so hard I forgot how to speak.

She laughed, embarrassed. “That sounded strange. I’ve been told I have a familiar face.”

“I’ve dreamed about you.”

Her smile faded. For a moment, the city’s rain fell through her hair without disturbing it. A rendering glitch. Nothing more.

“How many times?” she asked.

“Enough that I thought my brain had finally got bored of inventing new people.”

She looked down at her hands. “What happens in the dreams?”

“Nothing much. We’re always about to meet.”

“Oh,” she said.

A pause opened between us. In the real world, silence had weight. In Common Ground, it was easy to mistake silence for a dropped connection.

“Are you a person?” I asked.

She gave a short, humorless laugh. “That’s a terrible way to say hello.”

“I know. I’m sorry. It’s just—”

“You think I’m a dream character.”

“I think I might have made you.”

“Did you?”

“I don’t know.”

That, at least, was true. Simulations could build landscapes from a glance, voices from a few seconds of conversation. My own sleep rig sometimes turned fragments of the day into elaborate dreams. I’d once dreamed an entire city based on a bus ride. Why not a woman?

Lena studied me. “I have an account,” she said. “A name. A job I hate. Two sisters who send me pictures of their dogs. Is that enough?”

It wasn’t, and we both knew it.

She sent me a verification request. Her account was old, her identity credentials valid. I sent one back. Mine checked out too. The system gave us both a green ring.

A green ring meant the platform had verified our accounts. It didn’t mean we were sitting in the same room. It didn’t mean there wasn’t another layer underneath us, watching.

Still, we talked for an hour. Then another. When she logged off, the rain kept falling.

I dreamed of her that night.

This time, we were sitting on a bench beneath a bare tree. She told me her name was Lena. I told her mine. We were just about to say something important when I woke.

The next day, I messaged her.

She replied: *I dreamed about you too.*

We met in Common Ground again, then again. We learned each other’s habits. She liked terrible jokes and hated the city’s fake birds. I told her I collected dreams like other people collected old maps. She said that sounded lonely.

“What if you’re right?” she asked once. We were standing on a bridge over a river that neither of us had seen in person.

“About what?”

“That you made me.”

I looked at the water. It shone with perfect moonlight. “Then you’re a very good part of me.”

“That’s not the same as being real.”

“No,” I said. “It isn’t.”

We agreed to meet outside the sim.

The café she chose was small and loud and smelled of burnt coffee. I arrived early and picked a table by the window. For twenty minutes, every woman who entered made my heart jump.

Then Lena walked in.

No coat this time. No polished avatar, no perfect lighting. Just a woman with rain on her shoulders and the same scar at her chin.

She looked around, saw me, and smiled.

For a second I couldn’t move. The room was too detailed: chipped saucer, crooked menu, a child kicking the table behind me. Reality had always been like that, of course. But simulations had got very good.

“Hi,” she said.

“Hi.”

She sat down. “You’re staring.”

“I’ve dreamed of this.”

“Of coffee?”

“Of you.”

She laughed. The sound was rougher than her sim voice. Or maybe I had only imagined it that way.

We talked until the café closed. Afterward, beneath the awning, she took my hand. Her fingers were cold.

“Is this enough?” she asked.

I wanted to say yes. I wanted to say that the warmth of her palm, the rain, the ache in my chest were proofs no machine could counterfeit.

Instead, I said, “For tonight.”

She squeezed my hand.

And whether I was awake, or dreaming, or standing inside some newer world whose edges I couldn’t see, I was glad she was there.

content:
### The Quietest Breakfast

At 7:12 on Tuesday morning, the translator went down.

Mara knew because the little silver ring on her wrist stopped glowing—and because her husband, Jun, said something from across the kitchen that sounded like a flock of birds taking flight.

She stared at him.

Jun stared back. Then he tried again, slower, as if the problem might be his.

The ring gave a soft, apologetic chirp. **GLOBAL TRANSLATION SERVICE UNAVAILABLE. PLEASE STAND BY.**

From the table, their children began talking all at once.

Nico, eight, pointed at the cereal. Lila, five, held up a spoon and announced something urgent. Jun answered both of them. Mara understood none of it.

For twelve years, the translators had made everything easy. They had carried wedding vows, bedtime stories, arguments about laundry, and the complicated negotiations of raising children in three languages. Mara had learned only a handful of Jun’s words. There had always been time to learn more. The ring did it so well.

Now the kitchen was full of voices, and every one of them was a locked door.

Mara tapped her wrist. Nothing. Jun tapped his. Nothing.

Nico leaned over and pressed the table’s built-in hub. Its screen showed the same message. He frowned, then began speaking more loudly.

“Volume won’t fix it,” Mara said.

Nico looked at her blankly.

She demonstrated: pointed to her mouth, shook her head, then mimed turning a knob down. Nico grinned. He had understood enough.

Lila was still holding up her spoon. Her expression had gone from urgent to wounded.

Mara pointed at the spoon, then at the cereal box.

Lila shook her head and pointed toward the window.

“Outside?” Mara guessed.

Lila shook her head harder. She tapped the spoon against the glass, then made a small flapping motion with her hands.

“Bird,” Jun said.

Mara caught the word. She knew that one. She looked out the window. A bright red bird perched on the railing, pecking at a crumb.

Lila beamed. She pointed at the bird, then at Mara.

Mara smiled. “Yes. Bird.”

Jun said something that made Nico laugh. Mara didn’t know why. For a moment, annoyance rose in her, sharp and familiar: the feeling of being present but left out. She looked down at her coffee.

Then Jun reached across the table and covered her hand with his.

He said a word softly.

Mara knew that one, too. He had taught it to her years ago, back when they were dating and she wrote his words on scraps of paper. She had forgotten many. She had kept a few.

“Here,” he said—not in English, but in the language he had spoken to her when they first met.

Mara squeezed his fingers.

Nico began drawing on a napkin. He sketched the bird, then a little person beside it. Lila added a second person, with enormous hair. Jun drew a crooked sun. Mara added a coffee cup.

The children argued over the picture. Jun joined in. The words went past her, quick and musical, but their hands told the rest: a wing, a circle, a dramatic swoop over the imaginary breakfast table. Nico laughed so hard he nearly tipped his milk.

Mara listened. She watched their faces. When she missed a joke, Lila reached across and took her hand, then repeated it more slowly—not with words, but with an exaggerated flap of her arms.

Mara laughed anyway.

The ring blinked once. Then again.

A synthetic voice filled the kitchen. “Translation service restored.”

Jun’s next sentence appeared in Mara’s ear in perfect English. The children’s chatter became clear. Lila explained, at length, that the red bird had stolen a crumb and was therefore “a tiny breakfast thief.”

Mara smiled. She could understand every word now.

Still, she kept hold of Jun’s hand.

At the bottom of the napkin, beneath the bird and the crooked sun, she wrote one of the words he had taught her. She wasn’t sure the spelling was right.

Jun read it. His face softened.

Then he said another word. Slowly. Patiently.

Mara repeated it.

This time, the whole family understood.

prompt: You meet the man you could have been , and found that you do n't like him .
content:
### The Other Door

My mother’s house had two kitchens.

It was a trick of the renovations: one proper kitchen, with a stove and sink, and one narrow room behind it where she kept the old pantry shelves. When I was small, I believed the pantry door led somewhere else. I never found out where. By the time I came home to empty the house, the door had swollen shut.

I was trying to pry it open when a man behind me said, “You always did force things.”

I turned.

He had my face.

Not a face like mine. My face: the same crooked nose, the same pale scar through the left eyebrow, the same small notch in the chin from falling off my bicycle at nine. He was perhaps five years older, with gray at his temples and a suit that had been expensive before it became comfortable.

For a moment, I thought I was looking at a photograph of myself taken in a life I hadn’t lived.

“Who are you?” I asked.

He glanced at the pantry door. “You know.”

I didn’t. Then I did.

He was the me who’d stayed.

At nineteen, our father had asked me to come home and help run the hardware store. I’d had a scholarship to a university two states away. I chose the scholarship. I’d spent the years since telling myself it was the only choice that could have made me happy.

The other me had stayed. He’d taken over the store, looked after our parents, married a woman named Laura, and raised a daughter.

“You’re real?” I said.

He gave me a tired smile. “You always needed a lot of evidence.”

I disliked him at once.

He walked through the kitchen as if he owned it, which, in some sense, he did. He knew which cupboard held the tea and where Mother kept the good scissors. He knew that the tap had to be turned hard to the left before it would stop dripping.

“I took care of them,” he said, filling the kettle.

“I’m sure they appreciated it.”

“I’m sure they did, too.”

There it was: the invoice, folded neatly into his voice.

He told me the store had done well. He’d bought out the neighboring lot, expanded into garden supplies, then sold the business before the lumber market collapsed. He’d been a member of the town council. He’d chaired the hospital fundraiser. He spoke about all this without bragging, which made it sound like a list of duties he’d performed while the rest of us were out wasting our lives.

“And Laura?” I asked.

“Divorced.”

“I’m sorry.”

“Don’t be. She got the house.”

He said this with a little laugh, as if he’d been robbed of something he’d never wanted.

His daughter, he told me, was twenty-four. She lived in Portland. They spoke on her birthday.

“Why only then?”

He set two mugs on the table. “She’s busy.”

There was a pause, full of the things he could have said but didn’t.

“You were a good son,” I said.

He looked at me sharply. “You don’t get to say that.”

I felt my cheeks warm. I hadn’t meant it as praise. Or not only praise.

He leaned against the counter. “You left, and you made a life. Good for you. But don’t turn me into the version of you who did everything right.”

“I didn’t.”

“You’re sitting there admiring me.”

“I’m not.”

“You’re asking if the life you didn’t choose was better.”

I looked down at the tea. He’d made it exactly the way our mother had: one bag, too much milk, no sugar.

“And was it?” I asked.

He shrugged. “Better than what?”

He had my habit of answering a question with a question. It was one of the things I most disliked about myself.

He told me that when our father got sick, he’d stayed up nights beside him. He also told me he resented every hour of it. He said he’d wanted our father to notice the sacrifice, then hated him for not noticing, then hated himself for wanting to be thanked.

He said all this as if confessing to a priest he didn’t believe in.

“I thought you’d be happier,” I said.

“So did I.”

The house creaked around us. Somewhere in the walls, the old pipes knocked.

“You’re very easy to dislike,” I said.

He smiled. “That’s one thing we have in common.”

For a moment I saw him not as a better choice, or a worse one, but as a man who had spent his life carrying a weight and calling it virtue because he didn’t know what else to call it.

Then he looked at me and said, “Your daughter still thinks you’re too busy to call?”

I stood up so quickly the chair scraped the floor.

He’d guessed. Or he’d known. Either way, the words landed.

“I call her.”

“Sometimes.”

I hated him most then. Not for being cruel, but for knowing where to press. It was the sort of thing I did, too: find the bruise, then tell myself I was only being honest.

I went to the pantry door. The swollen wood resisted my shoulder. The other me came and stood beside me.

“Don’t,” he said. “It won’t open.”

“Maybe you never pushed hard enough.”

He gave a soft, humorless laugh. “Maybe.”

We pushed together. The door shifted with a long wooden groan. Behind it was only the pantry: dust, shelves, a jar of dried beans gone pale with age. Nothing beyond. No second life waiting in the dark.

When I turned, he was gone.

I called my daughter from the front steps. She answered on the fourth ring.

“Dad?”

“Hi,” I said. “I’m at Grandma’s. I was thinking about you.”

“You okay?”

I looked back at the house, at the two doors that had never led anywhere but in.

“I think so,” I said. “Can I come see you this weekend?”

There was a pause.

“Yeah,” she said. “I’d like that.”

I didn’t promise I’d be better. I didn’t explain the man I’d met. I only asked what time her train came in, and wrote it down so I wouldn’t forget.

content:
**The Last Shot**

With 2.1 seconds left in the championship game, the Harbor City Herons were down by one.

Milo Vance stood in the corner, caught the inbound pass, and rose for the shot that would make him a legend. The whole arena held its breath.

Then a T-shirt landed on the ball.

It wrapped around the spinning leather like a tiny blue parachute. The shot veered left, struck the rim, and bounced into the hands of the visiting team. The buzzer sounded. The Herons lost.

People blamed the shooter. The referee. The arena’s ventilation system, which had been acting strangely all night.

No one blamed me.

I was in Section 114, Seat 8, where the trouble began with a peppermint.

I’d unwrapped it during the final timeout and tucked the crinkled wrapper into the gap beside my seat. The wrapper jammed the folding armrest. When I stood to cheer, the armrest didn’t fold down. My rally towel caught on it, and when I yanked free, the towel flew over the row in front and landed on the head of a little boy.

The boy burst into tears. His father stood to comfort him, accidentally knocking a foam finger from his own hand. It bounced down the steps and landed beneath the shoe of a popcorn vendor.

The vendor slipped. He didn’t fall, exactly, but he pinwheeled into the Herons’ mascot, who was doing a spirited dance near the aisle. The mascot staggered backward, grabbed at the mascot head, and pulled it off.

The enormous blue heron head rolled down the steps.

It bumped the ankle of the T-shirt cannon operator, who was standing at the sideline, waiting for the final whistle. He flinched. His foot came down hard on the trigger.

The cannon fired.

A shirt arced over the court.

At that exact instant, Milo Vance released the shot.

The rest is history, though not the kind Harbor City wanted.

I have kept the peppermint wrapper. It sits in my desk drawer, folded into a neat little square. Sometimes I take it out and smooth it flat, as if that might undo anything.

I’ve considered telling someone. But who would believe me? The crowd saw a vendor stumble, a mascot lose his head, and a shirt fly at the wrong moment. They saw a missed shot.

Only I saw the whole chain.

And I’m fairly sure the wrapper is still stuck in that armrest.

content:
### The Match

The first time I saw the city burn, I was seven years old.

My mother held me on the roof while the old harbor went up in orange waves. The fire had started in a warehouse—an accident, the papers said. By morning, the warehouse was ash, three streets were gone, and the king had blamed the dockworkers.

My mother watched the smoke crawl over the rooftops.

“Fire doesn’t care who lit it,” she said. “Only who gets burned.”

At twenty-six, I was standing on that same roof with a matchbook in my pocket and a man beside me who believed the world deserved to burn.

“Once the gasworks go,” Rafe said, “the palace goes with them. No heat, no lights, no soldiers. The people will finally have a chance.”

Below us, the city glittered with lamps. Behind every lit window, someone was trying to sleep through the curfew sirens.

“You said the blast would take the west quarter.”

“It might.”

“There are children there.”

“There are children everywhere, Mara.”

He said it gently, as if kindness could make the words less ugly.

Rafe had once kissed me beneath the clock tower and promised we’d leave the city together. Then the king’s soldiers had taken his brother, and promises had given way to plans. He’d been planning ever since.

He reached for my hand. The matchbook in my pocket pressed against my thigh.

“Some men just want to watch the world burn,” he said, smiling sadly. “And darling, you’re the match.”

For a moment, I saw myself as he did: a spark in a dark room. A useful little thing. Something to strike and toss away.

Then I remembered my mother’s hands, blackened from carrying buckets to the harbor fire. I remembered that she’d gone back into the burning warehouse for a stranger’s child.

“I’m not your match,” I said.

Rafe’s smile faded. “Mara—”

I ran.

The gasworks stood at the river’s edge, a kingdom of iron pipes and sleeping flames. I knew its corridors from the years I’d spent repairing the lamps. I knew which valves fed the palace, which fed the west quarter, and which led to the old tunnels beneath the river.

Rafe caught up with me at the main control wheel.

“You can’t stop it,” he said. “The city has to change.”

“It does.”

“Then help me.”

“I am.”

I turned the wheel.

The pipes groaned. Deep beneath our feet, gas surged away from the crowded streets and into the abandoned tunnels. Rafe stared at the pressure gauges, understanding too late.

“You’re sending it under the river.”

“To the old flood chamber.”

“That chamber is sealed.”

“Not anymore.”

I struck a match.

Its tiny flame shivered in the damp air. Rafe stepped toward me, his face suddenly young again, the boy beneath the clock tower.

“Mara, don’t.”

I touched the flame to the fuse.

The explosion lifted us off our feet. The river jumped its banks in a silver wall. The gasworks’ eastern tower folded inward, and a column of fire burst up from the flood chamber—away from the homes, away from the palace, bright enough to turn every window in the city gold.

Then the lamps went out.

For one breath, the city was completely dark.

And then, one by one, lights appeared in the windows: candles, lanterns, torches. People opening their doors. People spilling into the streets. People seeing one another.

Rafe lay beside me, blood at his temple. He looked toward the rising flames.

“You started it,” he whispered.

“No,” I said, and helped him sit up. “I showed them where to look.”

Across the river, the palace bells began to ring. The crowd answered—not with a cheer, but with a thousand doors thrown open at once.

In my hand, the match had burned down to my fingertips.

I let it fall.

### The Other Side of Morning

At 5:12 a.m., you wake to the sound of your bones rearranging.

It starts behind your knees, a soft, private ache. Then your shoulders draw inward. Your jaw loosens. The rest follows—not pain, exactly, but the deep wrongness of a familiar room changing shape around you.

You lie still until it’s done.

Beside you, Daniel sleeps on his stomach, one arm flung across the empty half of the bed. Last night, he met you as a man: dark-haired, broad-shouldered, wearing a green shirt you’d stolen from a laundromat years ago. Tonight—now—it’s your turn to be a woman. The world has always insisted on making a schedule of you. One day here, one day there. You stopped trying to bargain with it.

You slide out from beneath the sheet.

Your clothes are in a loose pile beside the bed. The shirt is useless now; the shoulders hang too wide. Your jeans pool around your ankles. You find your underwear, then your boots, and carry them into the hallway. The apartment is unfamiliar in the gray light: a stack of books, a dying basil plant, a framed photo of Daniel grinning beside a woman with his eyes.

You’d asked about her last night. His sister, he’d said. Then he’d kissed you.

At the front door, you stop to put on your boots. The left one catches on your heel. You bite your lip to keep from swearing.

Behind you, the bed creaks.

You freeze.

“Hey,” Daniel says, voice thick with sleep.

You look at the door. The lock is one turn away. You could make it out. You’ve made it out of worse places, and without leaving a name behind.

“Sorry,” you whisper.

“For what?”

You don’t answer. His footsteps cross the room, slow and bare. You can feel the moment he sees you: the pause, the catch in his breath. You brace for the question you’ve learned to hate. What happened to you? Who are you? Which one are you really?

Instead, he says, “You’re leaving?”

You look back. Daniel is standing in the bedroom doorway, sheet wrapped around his waist. His eyes flick from your face to the oversized shirt in your hand, then back again. He looks startled. Of course he does. You are startled every morning.

“I should,” you say.

“Because of me?”

“Because of this.”

He glances at the shirt. “You mean the clothes?”

You almost laugh. It comes out as a thin breath. “I mean me.”

Daniel rubs his palm over his jaw. “Okay.”

The plainness of it unsettles you more than panic would have.

“You’re not going to ask?”

“I’m going to ask if you want coffee.” He hesitates. “And maybe, if you want to tell me, I’ll listen. But you don’t have to explain yourself before sunrise.”

You glance at the lock again.

“I’m not always…” You stop. There is no neat way to say it. There never has been. “I change.”

“Yeah,” he says softly. “I can see that.”

You wait for him to ask which version he’d slept with. Whether last night had been a trick. Whether you were one person or two, and which of you he’d liked.

He only steps aside, leaving the way to the door clear.

The kindness feels like another change you haven’t prepared for.

“I don’t stay,” you say.

“Then don’t.” He turns toward the kitchen. “But the coffee’s happening either way.”

You take one boot off. Then the other. It isn’t a promise. It isn’t even a decision to stay. Just a pause, a little room before the next thing.

In the kitchen, Daniel fills the kettle. The basil plant droops on the windowsill. The morning brightens by degrees, touching the counters, the mugs, the green shirt hanging from your fingers.

You sit at the table.

Daniel sets a cup in front of you. He doesn’t look away, and he doesn’t stare.

For once, the day can wait.

prompt: Description of your favourite meal
content:
### The Meal That Waited

My favourite meal begins with the sound of rain.

It taps at the kitchen window while a pot of chicken soup simmers on the stove. Inside, the broth turns golden around carrots, potatoes, and little curls of egg noodles. The whole house fills with its warm, peppery smell—the kind that seems to find you wherever you are and gently lead you home.

My grandmother used to make it on Sundays. She never measured anything. A pinch of salt, a shake of pepper, a handful of noodles: everything went into the pot by instinct. When I asked how she knew when it was ready, she would lift the lid, breathe in, and say, “It smells like enough.”

We ate at a small wooden table near the window. She always gave me the biggest bowl, though she pretended it was an accident. I would scoop up a spoonful and blow across it until it was cool enough to taste. The broth was rich but not heavy, and the noodles were soft, soaking up all its flavour. Each bite seemed to chase away the cold.

One Sunday, I arrived late. The rain had already stopped, and the soup was waiting on the stove. My grandmother had left a bowl on the table with a plate over it to keep it warm. Beside it was a note: **I knew you’d come hungry.**

She was right. I sat down and ate slowly, listening to the quiet house and thinking of all the Sundays we had shared. The meal tasted just as it always had—salty, savory, and comforting—but now I understood that its best ingredient had never been in the pot.

It was the feeling of being expected.

That is why chicken soup remains my favourite meal. Not because it is fancy, or difficult to make, but because every spoonful carries the same promise: no matter how cold the day has been, there is a warm bowl waiting for you.

prompt: Challenging the Behemoth Peak Spider
content:
# Challenging the Behemoth Peak Spider

By the time Tavi reached the last ridge, the mountain had swallowed the sun.

Behemoth Peak rose above the clouds in a jagged crown of black stone. Somewhere near its summit grew the blue frost-lily—the only flower that could cure Tavi’s brother. The village elders had warned him about the guardian.

“The spider is bigger than a house,” they said. “Its web can catch a falling boulder. No one who challenges it has ever returned.”

Tavi had packed rope, a pickaxe, and a knife. He had not packed a plan.

Then the ridge narrowed to a ledge, and there it was.

The Behemoth Peak Spider crouched across the path, its eight legs braced against the cliffs. Silver markings shone on its dark body. Strands of web stretched behind it, vanishing into the mist.

Tavi gripped his pickaxe. “I’ve come for a frost-lily.”

The spider’s many eyes blinked. Its voice was a low vibration in the stone.

“Then you must pass me.”

Tavi lifted his pickaxe. The spider didn’t move.

“Is this a fight?” he asked.

“Is that what you brought?”

Tavi glanced at the pickaxe, then at the webbing tangled across the mountain. One strand trembled in the wind. Another had snapped, leaving a long curtain of silver threads sagging over the ravine.

“I brought what I thought I’d need,” he said.

“And what do you need now?”

Tavi looked at the spider. “To get across.”

The creature shifted aside—not enough to let him pass, but enough to reveal a narrow gap in its web. Beyond it, the path continued up the mountain.

“Show me,” said the spider, “that you can cross without breaking what holds this peak together.”

Tavi studied the web. It was beautiful, but the storm had torn it in several places. Some strands ran from one cliff to another, taut as harp strings. Others dangled loose. The whole network trembled under the weight of the wind.

He had no idea how to repair it.

So he asked.

The spider taught him which threads could bear weight and which were only delicate supports. Tavi tied his rope around a stone tooth in the cliff and crawled along the ledge, reaching for the broken strands. The wind shoved him hard enough to make his boots skid. Twice, the spider caught him with a loop of silk before he could fall.

“Careful,” it rumbled.

“I am being careful.”

“You are being stubborn. There is a difference.”

Tavi almost laughed. “I’ve heard that before.”

Together they worked. The spider spun new threads, while Tavi tied them to the cliff anchors. His fingers grew numb. His shoulders burned. But as the web tightened, the path steadied beneath them.

At last, the silver curtain lifted clear of the ravine.

The spider stepped aside.

Tavi stood, breathing hard. “So I can pass?”

“You may.”

He began up the path, then stopped. “Why guard the frost-lilies if you don’t want to keep people away?”

The spider’s eyes reflected the first stars. “People come here with blades and ropes and take what they wish. The lilies grow where the mountain is weakest. Their roots hold the snow in place. Take too many, and the whole slope will fall.”

Tavi thought of his brother, pale and feverish in their little house. “I need one.”

“One flower,” said the spider. “Leave its roots, and the mountain will endure.”

At the summit, Tavi found the frost-lily growing between two stones, its blue petals glowing like moonlight. He cut the stem carefully, leaving the roots untouched.

When he returned, the spider was waiting.

“Did you find what you needed?” it asked.

“Yes,” said Tavi. “And I found out what I owe.”

He pointed to the web, shining strong across the ravine. “I’ll come back after the thaw and help repair the rest.”

The spider lowered its great head.

“Then you have challenged Behemoth Peak,” it said, “and the mountain has accepted your answer.”

Tavi tucked the flower safely inside his coat and began the long descent. Behind him, the spider’s web hummed softly in the wind—not like a trap, but like a song.

prompt: Instead of being born as a citizen , you must choose which country you wish to be a citizen of when you reach adulthood .
content:
### The Country on the Line

On the morning of her eighteenth birthday, Imani Vale woke to three passports on the kitchen table.

They were not real passports yet—just blue, green, and red sample booklets, each stamped with the seal of a country she could choose. At midnight, her childhood status would expire. Before then, she had to name the country whose citizen she would become.

The law called it the Open Choice. Every child, wherever they were born, grew up with the same temporary papers. At eighteen, they chose. No country could refuse them. No one could choose for them.

Imani’s mother had chosen Veyra, the mountain country where her own parents still lived. Her father had chosen Oran, across the sea, where he now worked on ships. Imani had grown up in Lydon, a low, bright city of ferries and floodwalls. She had never needed to belong to any of those countries to live there.

Now everyone had an opinion.

“Veyra has the best universities,” her mother said, turning the green passport toward her. “And your cousins are there.”

“Oran needs people who know the coast,” her father said over the kitchen screen. “You could do useful work. You’d be close to me.”

Imani looked at the blue passport, the one for Lydon. The city had taught her to ride a bicycle, swim in the harbor, and read the warning lights on the floodwall. It had also flooded her school twice.

“You don’t have to choose where you were born,” her mother said gently.

“I know.”

“You don’t have to choose us.”

“I know that, too.”

She packed a bag and took the ferry to the outer islands. The ferry’s captain, who had no citizenship until she’d turned eighteen, had chosen Lydon. So had the young man collecting fares. So had the old woman selling oranges from a cooler.

“Why Lydon?” Imani asked her.

The woman shrugged. “I like rain.”

“That’s your reason?”

“Do you need a better one?”

By afternoon, the water was rising. A storm had pushed the tide against the coast, and the ferries were ordered back to port. Imani helped the orange seller carry her cooler up the steps. At the top, they watched the sea slap at the lowest road.

“You could leave,” Imani said.

The woman glanced at her. “So could you.”

Imani thought about that all the way home.

At the city registry, a clerk sat behind a glass desk. On the wall, a clock counted down the hours until midnight.

“Any country in the world,” the clerk said. “You may change your mind until the form is sealed.”

Imani filled in her name. Then she paused at the line marked COUNTRY.

Her mother and father sat on either side of her. They had come, though neither had asked her to choose their country. Her mother held Imani’s hand beneath the desk. Her father rested his palm on the back of her chair.

Imani thought of Veyra’s mountains, blue in the photographs her mother sent. She thought of Oran’s harbor, where her father’s voice always sounded windblown. She thought of Lydon’s alleys, the corner shop where the owner saved the bruised peaches for children, and the neighbors who had carried sandbags to the floodwall without asking anyone’s passport.

She wrote Lydon.

The clerk took the form. “Do you understand that citizenship comes with obligations?”

“I do.”

“Taxes, jury service, and, if called, civil defense.”

“I know.”

The stamp came down with a soft thump.

Outside, the storm had passed. The streets shone with rain, and the harbor lights trembled in the puddles. Her mother kissed her cheek. Her father handed her the red and green sample passports to take home.

“You can visit,” he said.

“I will.”

The blue passport in her hand was still warm from the registry. It did not make Lydon safer. It did not make it fairer, or drier, or easier to love.

But it made the city hers to answer for.

At midnight, the old temporary papers went dark. Imani stood at her window and watched the tide withdraw from the streets.

For the first time, the country on the other side of the glass was not simply where she lived.

It was where she belonged—and where she would stay to help.

prompt: Tell me the story of how the first king became the first king
content:
Before there were kings, people settled wherever the earth was kind.

They lived beside a broad river that gave them fish, rich soil, and, once each spring, a flood. The flood was not a surprise. It was as dependable as sunrise, and nearly as dangerous.

Whenever the river began to rise, the people argued.

“Build the wall higher,” said the farmers.

“Leave the water room to spread,” said the fishers.

“Move the village uphill,” said the elders.

Everyone had a plan. Everyone spoke at once. And every year, while they argued, the river climbed.

One spring, the rain fell for seven days. On the eighth, the river broke through its banks and rushed toward the village.

A young potter named Enna heard the warning first. She ran from house to house, shouting for people to climb the hill. But some families went east, some west, and some refused to leave their homes. The flood swept away the first row of huts.

Then Enna climbed onto the old stone well and called out, “If you can hear me, carry the children uphill! If you have a boat, take the sick. If you have strong arms, break open the grain store and bring food!”

For a moment, everyone looked at everyone else.

Then they began.

The fishers gathered the children. The farmers hauled the grain. The elders guided the slow and the frightened. Enna sent people where they were needed, and the village moved as one body. By nightfall, every person was safe on the hill.

In the morning, they looked down at the place where their homes had stood. The river had taken nearly everything.

“We need someone to decide what we do next,” said a farmer.

“We need someone who will listen,” said a fisher.

“We need someone who won’t wait until the water is at the door,” said an elder.

They turned to Enna.

She shook her head. “I’m a potter. I don’t want to command anyone.”

“Then don’t command us,” said the eldest woman. “Help us decide. And when we cannot decide, choose the path that keeps us alive.”

So Enna helped them build again, this time on higher ground. She asked every household where the new paths should run. She marked places for food, shelter, and boats. She made rules for the riverbank—and agreed that the people could change those rules if they proved unfair.

When the village was finished, the people gathered beneath an ash tree. They wanted a name for the one who would speak for the whole village, settle disputes, and remember what had been promised.

They chose the word *king*.

Enna laughed when they offered it to her. “Does a king get a bigger house?”

“No,” they said.

“More food?”

“No.”

“Then what does a king get?”

“The first duty,” said the eldest woman.

So Enna accepted. They placed a plain circlet of woven reeds on her head—not gold, not jewels, just reeds from the river that had nearly taken them all.

And that is how the first king became king: not by conquering a people, but by helping them become one.

prompt: Timeline of Events
content:
# Timeline of Events

**8:03 a.m.**  
Mara found the envelope beneath her apartment door.

Her name was written across the front in her own handwriting. Inside was a single sheet of paper titled **TIMELINE OF EVENTS**.

**8:17 a.m.**  
Mara laughed, put the page in her coat pocket, and left for work.

**9:42 a.m.**  
At the city archives, she unfolded the paper again. A new line had appeared.

**10:06 a.m. — Mara will receive a phone call from her brother. She will not answer.**

Her brother, Daniel, had been dead for three years.

At 10:06, the phone on Mara’s desk rang. The screen showed **DANIEL**—the number she’d never had the heart to delete.

She let it ring.

**10:07 a.m.**  
The paper changed.

**Mara answers.**

Mara snatched up the phone. “Hello?”

For a moment there was only breathing. Then Daniel said, “You always were late.”

She gripped the receiver so hard her fingers hurt. “This isn’t possible.”

“Probably not,” he said. “But you need to listen. Tonight, don’t go home.”

The line crackled.

“Daniel—”

**10:08 a.m.**  
The call ended.

Mara stared at the page. A fresh line appeared beneath the others.

**6:31 p.m. — Mara will ignore the warning.**

She spent the day trying to prove the paper was a trick. She searched the archives for the phone number, checked the call log, and asked the operator to trace it. There was no call. There had never been one.

At 6:20, she stood outside the archive doors with the paper trembling in her hand.

The next line read:

**6:31 p.m. — A fire will begin in Mara’s apartment building.**

Mara called emergency services. They asked whether she could see smoke. She couldn’t. She asked her neighbor to check her stove. The neighbor said everything was fine.

At 6:29, Mara ran home.

At 6:31, the building alarm began to scream.

Smoke poured from the second-floor hallway. Mara’s neighbor, Mrs. Alvarez, was trapped behind her jammed apartment door. Mara and a firefighter pulled her out just before the ceiling collapsed.

By midnight, the fire was out. No one had died.

Mara unfolded the page under the flashing red lights. The final line had vanished. In its place, new words appeared.

**Tomorrow, 8:03 a.m. — Mara will find an envelope beneath her door.**

She looked up at her scorched building, then back at the page.

A small note appeared at the bottom.

**Some events can be changed. Some can only be witnessed.**

Mara folded the paper and put it away.

For the first time in three years, she was glad she had answered the phone.
