prompt: An assassin describing their weapon of choice in vivid detail .
content:
My weapon of choice was a knife called Mercy.

It was not a beautiful knife. Beautiful things invite admiration, and admiration makes people careless. Mercy was plain: a narrow, dark blade, a dull silver guard, a handle worn smooth where my thumb rested. In lamplight, it showed no shine—only a thin seam of gray, like winter showing through a crack in a door.

I kept it wrapped in blue cloth inside the lining of my coat. The cloth had once belonged to my mother. It smelled faintly of cedar, though I’d long ago forgotten whether the cedar was real or only memory.

People imagine an assassin’s weapon must be clever. They ask about hidden mechanisms, special alloys, poisons with picturesque names. They want a weapon that explains the person holding it.

Mercy explained nothing.

On the night I was meant to use it, rain stitched silver lines down the windows of the Halcyon Hotel. My target was in the ballroom beneath me, laughing among diplomats beneath a ceiling painted with clouds. I could hear the orchestra through the floor: violins, bright and brittle as ice.

I had watched the man for six weeks. Learned the tilt of his head when he listened, the small pause before he lied. He wore a red carnation in his lapel. He had a daughter, I’d been told. A little girl with a gap between her front teeth.

At midnight, he stepped onto the balcony alone.

I followed with Mercy in my hand.

He didn’t turn when I came through the glass doors. “You’re late,” he said.

The rain cooled the back of my neck. Behind him, the city blurred into rivers of gold and black.

“I expected you to run,” I said.

“I’m tired of running.”

I unwrapped the knife. The blue cloth fluttered once in the wind and caught on the balcony rail. For a moment, my mother’s old fabric waved between us like a flag from a country neither of us could return to.

He looked at the blade, then at me.

“Is that what you call it?” he asked.

“Mercy.”

A faint smile crossed his face. “Then you’ve brought the wrong thing.”

He reached into his coat. I raised the knife.

But what he drew out was a photograph, soft at the corners from being handled. A little girl stood in a garden, missing-toothed grin bright as a lantern. On the back, in careful handwriting, was my name.

My real name.

The orchestra below swelled. The rain kept writing its silver lines.

I lowered Mercy.

The man set the photograph on the rail between us. “They told you I was a monster,” he said. “They tell everyone that.”

I looked at the blade in my palm: dark, quiet, patient. For the first time, it seemed less like a weapon than a question.

Then I folded the blue cloth around it and put it away.

Downstairs, the music ended. The applause rose like a storm.

prompt: A woman you casually know spots you as you walk through a store , approaches you , smiles and says , `` I saw your gravestone today , just lovely ! '' and nonchalantly strolls away .
content:
The woman was called Diane, though I couldn’t have said where I knew her from. She was one of those people who belonged to the edges of your life: a face at the pharmacy, a familiar voice at the school fundraiser, someone you’d once stood beside in the rain.

I was comparing two jars of pasta sauce when she came up behind me.

“I saw your gravestone today,” she said, smiling. “Just lovely!”

For a moment I thought I’d misheard her.

“My what?”

But Diane was already pushing her cart away. She gave a little wave over her shoulder and turned down the next aisle, as casually as if she’d complimented my shoes.

I stood there with a jar in each hand.

At home, I looked her up online. There were several Dianes in town. None of them seemed like the sort to joke about gravestones. I told myself she’d meant someone else. Someone with my first name, perhaps. Someone whose grave she’d visited by accident.

Still, I didn’t sleep well.

The next morning I drove to St. Bartholomew’s Cemetery. It was the only cemetery nearby with a stonecutter’s workshop. I asked the woman in the office if anyone had ordered a headstone under my name. She checked the ledger and shook her head.

“Not that I see.”

I thanked her and started back to the car.

Then I noticed the fresh earth.

It lay in a narrow rectangle between two old maples, dark and neat against the winter grass. At its head stood a pale stone, too new to have gathered even a speck of moss.

My name was carved across it.

Below that was my birth date. Beneath that, a date that was one day away.

The inscription read: SHE WAS ALWAYS ON HER WAY HOME.

I touched the letters. The stone was cold.

“Is it yours?” someone asked.

I turned. A groundskeeper was watching me from the path.

“I don’t know,” I said.

He looked at the stone, then at me. “It’s been there a while.”

“How long?”

He shrugged. “Long enough.”

I went home and locked the door. I called my sister, but couldn’t bring myself to explain. I called the cemetery office again. The woman said the ledger still showed nothing.

That night, I slept on the sofa with every light on.

In the morning, I went back.

The grave was still there. So was the stone. My death date had not changed.

I stood among the bare trees, listening to the wind move through them. Then I noticed something tucked beneath the stone: a small white card, damp at the corners.

On it, in tidy handwriting, was one sentence:

I’M SO GLAD YOU LIKE IT.

I looked toward the cemetery gate.

Diane was walking away, her hands in the pockets of her coat. She didn’t turn around. The snow began to fall, softening the path behind her.

I ran after her, but by the time I reached the gate, the road was empty.

content:
At 11:47 p.m., Mara found a door in the laundromat that hadn’t been there before.

It stood between the change machine and the vending machine, narrow and blue, with a brass knob shaped like a sleeping bird. The dryers turned behind her, full of other people’s warm, anonymous clothes.

Mara checked the door for a sign. There was none.

She opened it.

On the other side was a beach beneath a green moon. Waves came in quietly, carrying little silver fish that vanished into the sand. A man in a yellow raincoat sat at the water’s edge, writing in a notebook.

“You’re late,” he said.

Mara looked back. Through the doorway she could see the laundromat, the flickering lights, the dryer where her red scarf went around and around.

“Late for what?”

The man closed his notebook. “For deciding.”

She laughed, because it was the sort of thing people said when they had been waiting too long. “I’m not deciding anything.”

“Then you can go back.”

Behind her, the laundromat hummed. The scarf tumbled. The vending machine dropped a bottle with a thunk, though nobody had touched it.

Mara stepped onto the beach.

The man stood and handed her the notebook. Its pages were blank except for one sentence, written in her own handwriting:

*I’m going to call him tomorrow.*

She had written that sentence a hundred times. On receipts. In the margins of books. Once on the fogged bathroom mirror, where it disappeared before she could photograph it.

The man watched her read.

“Is this a trick?” she asked.

“No,” he said. “It’s a beach.”

The green moon shivered on the water. Mara thought of her father’s voice, years old and still waiting in a message she hadn’t listened to since the hospital. She thought of all the tomorrows she had stored up, bright and unused as coins.

She took out her phone.

There was no signal. Of course there wasn’t. The screen showed the time: 11:47 p.m.

Mara looked at the man. “What happens if I don’t?”

“Nothing,” he said. “That’s the trouble.”

She opened the old message.

At first there was only static, then her father clearing his throat, then the ordinary sound of him saying her name. He asked whether she was still making soup the way he taught her. He told her the rain had finally stopped. He said he loved her, though he said it quickly, as if embarrassed by the words.

The message ended.

The waves kept coming. The moon kept shining. The man in the yellow coat was already writing again.

When Mara turned around, the blue door was still there.

She went back through it. In the laundromat, her scarf had finished its cycle. She folded it carefully, then called the number she knew by heart.

Someone answered on the fourth ring.

“Hello?” said a voice, surprised and sleepy.

Mara held the phone close. “It’s me.”

For a moment, neither of them said anything.

Then the dryers went on turning, full of warm, anonymous clothes, and outside the window the night became a little less dark.

content:
**The Candidate With No Face**

At 8:03 on a Tuesday morning, Reddit announced it was running for president.

The announcement appeared everywhere at once: on the front page, in cooking forums, under a video of a raccoon stealing a sandwich, and in a thread titled *Is anyone else worried about the moon?*

**WE ARE REDDIT,** it said. **WE HAVE LISTENED TO THE PEOPLE.**

“Which people?” asked a journalist.

The statement received 87,000 upvotes and no reply.

Reddit’s campaign headquarters occupied a former shopping mall. The campaign manager was a moderator in a faded hoodie. The communications director was a bot that had been banned from three states. The candidate itself was represented by a glowing orange Snoo head mounted on a podium.

Its platform was ambitious.

Free healthcare, unless the healthcare discussion was locked.

A four-day workweek, pending review by a committee that had not yet been formed.

A national infrastructure plan voted on by the public, then overturned by a smaller vote in a different thread.

“Reddit understands the people,” declared the campaign manager. “We contain every kind of person.”

This was true. Reddit contained mechanics and microbiologists, teenagers and retirees, amateur historians, professional arguers, and one man who had posted the same photograph of a sandwich for eleven years. It contained people who wanted lower taxes and people who wanted higher taxes, people who wanted the country to slow down and people who wanted to build a rocket immediately.

It also contained a surprising number of people who believed they could run the country better than anyone currently running it.

At the first debate, Reddit took the stage.

“Mr. Reddit,” said the moderator, “how would you handle a national emergency?”

The orange Snoo glowed.

**FIRST, WE WOULD MAKE A MEGATHREAD.**

The crowd applauded. Then booed. Then applauded again when someone posted a compelling infographic.

“And what if the emergency required immediate action?”

**WE WOULD ASK THE COMMUNITY.**

“What if the community disagreed?”

**WE WOULD SORT BY TOP.**

The other candidates laughed. Reddit did not. It had no face to laugh with.

On election night, the results came in slowly, because the vote-counting website had been redesigned by people who thought the old one was “too cluttered.”

Reddit won several states decisively. It lost others to a candidate who promised fewer notifications. In the close states, the totals changed every time a new subreddit discovered the election.

At midnight, the networks called it.

Reddit had won.

For one glorious moment, the country celebrated. People cheered in the streets. The front page filled with victory posts. Someone made a cake shaped like the Constitution. Someone else explained why the cake was technically wrong.

Then came the first question of the transition:

Who would be vice president?

Reddit held a vote.

The top choice was a beloved children’s book character. The second was a golden retriever. The third was “nobody, but with a cool hat.”

The election commission rejected all three.

Reddit appealed.

For the next week, the country watched as the president-elect argued with itself. The finance committee wanted to cut spending. The history forum insisted the entire budget had been done before and provided links. A hobbyist community proposed solving the deficit with beekeeping. The moderators tried to maintain order, but every time they locked a thread, a new one appeared with the title **DISCUSSION CONTINUES HERE**.

At last, on Inauguration Day, Reddit rolled up to the Capitol on a small platform with wheels. The platform was pushed by three tired moderators and a volunteer who kept stopping to take pictures.

The new president looked out over the crowd.

“Do you swear to uphold the Constitution?” asked the chief justice.

A thousand voices answered at once.

**YES.**

**NO.**

**SOURCE?**

**THIS.**

The chief justice waited.

At last, one small voice rose above the others. It belonged to a user who had joined only to ask how to remove a stain from a carpet.

“Yes,” the voice said.

The crowd fell quiet.

The orange Snoo turned toward them.

For once, there was no vote, no poll, no argument about whether the carpet stain was actually paint.

Reddit raised its hand and took the oath.

Then, before the ceremony was over, someone posted a thread asking whether the new president’s hand had looked weird.

It received twelve thousand comments.

And, beneath it, the country began.

Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: Since the beginning heroes only die when they choose someone else to take their place . You 're one of the oldest living heroes . When deciding if you should pick a successor at random you receive a letter from an old friend that says : `` We are the only ones left '' It 's written in blood .
content:
### The Last Choice

The lottery drum was older than the country.

It stood in the Hall of Names, its brass sides polished by generations of nervous hands. Inside were slips bearing the names of everyone who had ever sworn to defend another person. Volunteer firefighters. Doctors. Soldiers. A schoolteacher who’d once stood between her students and a gunman.

Mara had written each name herself.

She had outlived every hero who came before her. She had watched kingdoms become countries, countries become borders on maps, and borders become arguments. She had not aged in two hundred and seventeen years.

Heroes, the old saying went, could only die by choosing someone else to take their place.

Mara had never chosen.

She was turning the drum’s handle when the messenger arrived with a letter.

The envelope was damp and dark. The words on it had been written in blood.

**Mara,  
We are the only ones left.  
Come before I choose.  
—Tomas**

She knew the handwriting. She had watched Tomas write it on treaty papers, battle plans, and once, in the dust of a ruined city, the name of a girl they’d failed to save.

Mara left the lottery drum turning.

She found him in the old railway station, beneath a clock stopped at 4:12. Tomas sat against a pillar, one hand pressed to his side. Blood seeped between his fingers. His face was gray with pain, but his eyes were bright.

“You’re late,” he said.

“You wrote in blood.”

“I couldn’t find a pen.”

Mara knelt beside him. “Who did this?”

“A collapsing roof. I was helping people out.”

“Of course you were.”

For a moment they smiled at each other. It felt like being young again, which for them meant only a few centuries of sorrow.

Then Mara saw the empty platform, the dust, the one battered suitcase beside him.

“Everyone else?” she asked.

“Gone,” said Tomas. “Chosen their successors, one by one. You know that.”

“I know.”

“They didn’t leave us a council. Or a rulebook. Or even a decent chair.”

“You always hated chairs.”

“I hated the way you sat in them.”

The joke thinned into silence.

Mara looked at his wound. “You’ll heal.”

“Eventually.”

“You have time.”

“Not if I choose.”

She glanced at him. “You’ve found someone?”

“I’ve found hundreds of people. That’s the trouble.” He took his hand from the wound. The blood beneath it was almost black. “You’re drawing a name at random.”

“I thought it was fair.”

“It’s easy.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“No,” he said. “It isn’t.”

The old station creaked around them. Outside, the city went on making its ordinary noises—traffic, distant music, someone calling a dog home.

“I don’t want to decide who deserves this,” Mara said.

“Then don’t.”

“I don’t want to make another person carry what I’ve carried.”

“Then ask them.”

She almost laughed. “You think a person can understand what we’re asking?”

“I think they should get the chance to say no.”

Tomas closed his eyes. For a moment she thought he’d slipped away, but then he spoke.

“There was a paramedic at the station. Leila. She stayed after the roof came down. Went back in twice. The second time, she knew the ceiling was coming.”

“She saved you?”

“She saved three people. I was incidental.”

“You’ve chosen her?”

“I have.”

The words were quiet. They changed the air between them.

Mara reached for his hand. “Tomas—”

“I’m not asking you to agree. I’m telling you before I do it.” His thumb brushed her knuckles. “I don’t want to disappear without saying goodbye.”

“You could have waited.”

“I’ve waited long enough.”

She wanted to tell him not to be noble. Not to make one more choice for everyone else. Instead, she held his hand.

Tomas looked toward the station entrance, where a young woman in a red jacket was speaking to an injured child. Mara had seen her earlier. She was tying a bandage with steady fingers, even though her own sleeve was soaked with blood.

“Leila,” Tomas said.

The young woman looked up.

Tomas drew a breath. “I choose you to take my place.”

The station seemed to hold still.

He exhaled, and the pain left his face. His hand grew light in Mara’s. The blood on his shirt became only blood.

Leila stared at them. “What did you just say?”

Mara bowed her head over her friend’s hand.

For a long while, she did not move.

Then she stood and walked to the young woman. She told her what the choice meant: the long years, the impossible rescues, the days when no one would thank her and the nights when she would remember everyone she hadn’t saved.

Leila listened. She looked down at the child she’d bandaged, then at Tomas.

“I don’t know if I’m brave enough,” she said.

“You don’t have to be brave right now,” Mara replied. “You only have to decide.”

Leila looked at the blood on her sleeve. “Then I’ll decide tomorrow.”

Mara smiled. “Good.”

Back at the Hall of Names, the lottery drum had stopped turning.

Mara took every slip from inside it and set them on the table. She would not choose a stranger at random. She would meet the people whose names she had gathered. She would tell them the truth. She would give them time.

And when one of them said yes—truly yes—Mara would let herself die.

Outside, the first pale light of morning touched the city.

For the first time in centuries, the world did not feel like something she had to hold up alone.

prompt: Hawksbill Mountain
content:
At dawn, Hawksbill Mountain looked like the back of something enormous sleeping beneath the clouds.

Mara had climbed it once as a child, with her father. She remembered the steep path, the cold orange slices he’d packed, and how the cliffs seemed to drop straight into the morning. Mostly, though, she remembered his promise.

“When you’re ready,” he’d said, “we’ll come back and watch the sun go down.”

He never got the chance.

Now Mara was thirty, and the promise had followed her through three apartments, two jobs, and a year of unopened letters from the lawyer. The last letter had contained a map of the mountain, drawn by her father on the back of an old receipt. At the summit he had marked a small X.

So, on the first clear Saturday in October, she drove to the trailhead alone.

The climb was steeper than she remembered. Roots crossed the path like knotted fingers. Leaves skittered under her boots. More than once, she stopped to catch her breath and considered turning around. But she kept going, partly for her father and partly because she was tired of treating grief as a locked room.

Near the top, she found the fallen pine.

It lay beside the trail, silver-gray and hollowed with age. Her father had made her sit on it when she was little, claiming it was a bench built for mountain explorers. She sat now, though the bark crumbled under her hand.

A breeze moved through the trees. Somewhere below, a crow called once, then went quiet.

Mara took the old receipt from her pocket. The pencil marks had faded, but the X was still visible. It pointed toward the overlook.

She reached it just as the sun began to sink. The mountains rolled away in blue and purple ridges, each one softer than the last. Far below, the gorge held the day’s remaining light in its shadowed folds.

Mara found no treasure at the X. No box, no message tucked beneath a stone. Only a flat slab of rock and a view so wide it made her feel, for the first time in months, less like the center of a disaster.

She sat down.

The sun touched the far ridge. Gold spilled along the clouds, then thinned to rose. Mara took the orange she’d packed from the car—one of the small, sharp ones her father used to bring—and peeled it slowly. Its scent rose bright in the cold air.

She ate one segment. Then another.

“I’m here,” she said.

The mountain gave no answer. It didn’t need to. Wind brushed her cheek, carrying the smell of leaves and stone. Behind her, the trail waited for the walk down. Ahead, the light disappeared one quiet color at a time.

Mara stayed until the first star appeared.

Then she folded the receipt along its old creases and put it back in her pocket. The X had not been a place to find something her father left behind. It had been a place to return to—with or without him.

At the trailhead, the car’s headlights blinked on as she opened the door. For a moment, she looked back.

Hawksbill Mountain stood dark against the sky, no longer asleep, but keeping watch.

prompt: [ NSFW ] The number of times someone has had sex is listed above their heads at all times for everyone to see . Describe a day in the life of a 50 year old virgin .
content:
At 7:03 on Tuesday morning, Arthur Bell stood in his bathroom and watched the small, glowing **0** hover above his head in the mirror.

It had been there for fifty years. It followed him into showers, job interviews, funerals, and the dentist’s chair. It showed up in every photograph, usually between his hair and the top of the frame. There was no way to hide it—not with hats, not with clever angles, not even with the enormous paper crown his niece had once made him for his birthday.

Arthur had tried a hat anyway. He put one on, checked the mirror, and sighed.

The **0** floated neatly above it.

“Good morning to you, too,” he said.

On the bus, the numbers bobbed over the other passengers’ heads. A **6** slept against the window. A **1** scrolled on her phone. A **23** clutched a bouquet, looking nervous. Arthur looked out at the passing shops and tried not to do what everyone did: add up other people’s lives from a single digit.

At the library, where he worked in local history, the new volunteer introduced herself as June. Her number was a **0**, like his.

She saw him notice.

“Twins,” she said.

Arthur smiled. “I was going to say we should start a club, but then we’d have to decide whether the club was about the number or not talking about the number.”

“Sounds like a very quiet club.”

Their first task was sorting a box of old photographs. They spent the morning guessing the names of people whose faces had been forgotten by everyone alive. Arthur liked June’s laugh. She liked the way he could identify a street from a corner of a photograph.

At lunch, she asked, “Do you mind if I ask about the zero?”

Arthur set down his sandwich. He had prepared for this question for decades and somehow never settled on an answer.

“Not usually,” he said. “I mind when people decide what it means before I’ve said anything.”

June nodded. Her own zero stayed steady above her head.

“And what does it mean?” she asked.

He considered the neat, impossible answer. That he’d been waiting for the right person. That he’d been too busy. That he’d never met anyone who wanted him. Each was partly true, which made none of them quite honest.

“Mostly that it hasn’t happened,” he said. “I don’t know if I want it to. I think I’d like to find out without treating it like a deadline.”

June smiled. “That seems reasonable.”

It was such a small response that Arthur felt something loosen in his chest.

After work, he went to the grocery store. A child in the cereal aisle pointed at Arthur’s **0** and asked her father what it meant. The father hurried her away, embarrassed. Arthur picked up a box of oats and let them go. He wasn’t angry. He was tired of being treated as either a mystery or a lesson.

At home, he called his sister to ask about their mother’s appointment. He watered the basil on the windowsill. He ate soup from a mug and watched a documentary about shipwrecks. His life, viewed from the inside, did not resemble a blank space. It was full of people he loved, books he’d read, places he’d been, and ordinary Tuesdays he had made it through.

At 8:41, his phone buzzed.

**June:** I enjoyed sorting the photographs with you. Would you like to get coffee sometime? No archival boxes required.

Arthur looked up. The **0** hovered over him, patient as ever.

He typed, erased, and typed again.

**Arthur:** I’d like that. Coffee sounds good.

Then, after a moment:

**Arthur:** For the record, I may be awkward.

Her reply came quickly.

**June:** I work in a library. Awkward is practically a qualification.

Arthur laughed aloud. The number over his head did not change. It wasn’t supposed to—not because of a text, or a good day, or the possibility of another one.

Still, for the first time in a long while, he went to bed thinking less about what the **0** announced and more about what tomorrow might bring.

prompt: A group of fantasy creatures are playing a table top game together where they pretend to be modern-day humans
content:
### No Magic Allowed

The sign on the tavern door read **CLOSED FOR ADVENTURING**.

Inside, five fantasy creatures sat around a table littered with dice, snacks, and one very stern-looking rulebook.

“No spells,” said Sable the sphinx, who was running the game. “No claws, no flight, no enchanted objects. You are all ordinary humans.”

Brindle the dragon tucked his wings under his chair. “How ordinary?”

“You have jobs, rent, and a group chat you’d rather mute.”

The goblin Nix nodded gravely. “Terrifying.”

Sable passed around character sheets. Brindle became Kevin, an accountant who lived in a third-floor apartment and owned a houseplant he’d named Gerald. Nix played Priya, a nurse finishing a long shift. Thistle the dryad became June, a bus driver with a passion for community gardening. Orro the ogre was Martin, a shy librarian. Pip the sprite—who was technically not allowed to fly but kept hovering an inch above her seat—played Alex, a barista.

Sable tapped the map. “It’s Saturday afternoon. Your apartment building is holding a rooftop gathering to watch the meteor shower. Then a storm knocks out the power.”

“Can Kevin breathe fire?” Brindle asked.

“No.”

“Can he at least be good at something?”

“He’s very good at spreadsheets.”

Brindle sighed. “Cruel.”

The game began.

Priya arrived home from work to find the elevator dead and an elderly neighbor stranded on the fifth floor. June was downstairs, trying to keep the storm from flooding the basement. Martin had the only working flashlight, but it was tucked inside a box of donated books. Alex was on the roof, guarding three trays of cupcakes from the wind.

“And Kevin?” Sable asked.

Brindle glanced at his character sheet. “Kevin is in his apartment, reorganizing his receipts.”

“Why?”

“He doesn’t know anyone in the building.”

“Your neighbor, Mrs. Alvarez, knocks on his door. She needs help carrying a box upstairs.”

Brindle frowned. “Kevin says he’s busy.”

The others groaned.

“What?” said Brindle. “He’s a realistic modern human.”

“He’s a modern human with a very good excuse to be useful,” said Nix.

Brindle looked again at the little drawing of Kevin on his sheet: a tired man in a sweater, holding a mug. “Fine. He goes.”

Kevin carried the box up five flights of stairs. Inside were folding chairs for the rooftop gathering. On the fourth floor, he met Martin, who had found the flashlight and was searching for the building’s fuse box. On the second, Priya offered them both leftover dumplings from her lunch.

Soon everyone was moving through the dark hallway together.

“June gets the basement pump working,” Thistle said. “She knows where the shutoff valve is because she’s been growing tomatoes down there.”

“Why are there tomatoes in the basement?” asked Sable.

“Because June is a bus driver, not a gardener. She made mistakes.”

“Fair.”

Up on the roof, Alex had secured the cupcakes beneath an umbrella. Kevin arrived with the chairs. Martin brought the flashlight. Priya brought the dumplings. June came last, soaked to the knees and carrying a bucket of rainwater she’d collected by accident.

The lights flickered back on.

For a moment, everyone at the table cheered.

Then Sable said, “The storm clears. The meteor shower begins. What do you do?”

Brindle considered Kevin, the accountant who had spent the whole game avoiding his neighbors.

“He asks Mrs. Alvarez if she wants to sit with them.”

Nix smiled. “She does.”

“And Kevin gives her the chair he carried upstairs.”

“Excellent,” said Sable. “The first meteor streaks across the sky.”

Pip leaned over the map. “Alex makes a wish.”

“On what?” asked Orro. “The meteor?”

“Sure.”

“What does Alex wish for?”

Pip thought for a moment. “That the power stays on.”

Sable shook her head. “That’s not very ambitious.”

“It’s been a long week.”

When the game ended, the tavern’s hearth had burned low. Outside, rain tapped softly on the windows. Brindle gathered his dice, careful not to scorch the table with his tail.

“I still don’t understand why humans do all that,” he said. “Stairs. Receipts. Small talk.”

“Because sometimes,” said Orro, “the only way to get something done is to carry a chair up five flights and hope someone saves you a dumpling.”

Everyone considered this.

“Next week,” said Sable, “you’re all humans again.”

“Can Kevin have a cat?” Brindle asked.

“Maybe.”

“Can the cat breathe fire?”

“No.”

Brindle tucked his character sheet into his coat. “Then I’ll have to make it work.”

prompt: A person 's final thoughts .
content:
The last thing Mara heard was the kettle.

It clicked off in the kitchen, though she hadn’t made tea in three days. For a moment she was certain she should get up and pour it. The thought came with such ordinary urgency that she almost laughed.

Then she remembered she was in the hospital, and the kettle was at home.

Home rose around her—not as a place, but as a collection of small, stubborn things. The chipped blue mug. The loose board by the back door. Her son Daniel, at nine, insisting that the moon followed their car because it liked him best.

She had never told him that, years later, she sometimes looked for it too.

Daniel sat beside her bed now, older than she had ever imagined he could become. His hand covered hers. He was saying something about the garden, about how the roses had survived the winter. Mara tried to answer, but the words had become difficult, like furniture in a dark room.

So she thought instead.

She thought of the things she’d saved and the things she’d thrown away. Of apologies she had made too late, and one she had never managed to make at all. She thought of the summer she and Daniel slept in a tent in the backyard, waking at dawn with damp grass beneath them and nowhere they needed to be.

Mostly, she thought how love had disguised itself. As packed lunches. As waiting up. As pretending not to notice when Daniel came home with muddy shoes. As all the years she had mistaken worry for its own separate thing.

His thumb moved across her knuckles.

“I’m here, Mom,” he said.

Mara wanted to tell him she knew. She wanted to tell him that he had been here all along, even when the miles and the silences made it hard to see.

The room grew quiet. Somewhere beyond the window, a bird called once, then again.

Mara imagined the kettle cooling on the counter. She imagined Daniel finding the blue mug, perhaps filling it, perhaps leaving it where it was. She imagined the moon above the house, following him home.

And as the last of the day slipped gently from her, she thought: *There you are.*

prompt: Professor Paradox manipulates time so that his defeat would cause a paradox
content:
At exactly 4:17 p.m., every clock in the city stopped.

The traffic lights froze between red and green. A flock of pigeons hung motionless above the courthouse. Even the rain paused in midair, each drop a glass bead suspended over the streets.

Mara looked up from the watch on her wrist. Its hands were spinning backward.

“Professor Paradox,” she said.

A man in a white suit stepped out of the frozen rain. He carried a pocket watch in one hand and a teacup in the other. The tea steamed upward, then curled into the cup again.

“Miss Vale,” he said. “You’re learning.”

“You stopped time.”

“Not quite. I’ve persuaded it to wait.”

Mara glanced at the silver machine strapped to his back. Rings turned around it at angles that made her eyes ache. “And if I take that off you?”

Paradox smiled. “Then you defeat me.”

“Sounds simple.”

“It would be, if you were able to do it.”

He tapped his watch. The city shivered. For a moment, Mara saw two versions of the street: one empty, one crowded; one beneath a bright summer sun, another under a black sky full of stars. Then they snapped together.

Paradox continued, “I have arranged matters so that my defeat causes a paradox. Should you remove the machine, I will never have built it. Without the machine, I cannot travel back to prevent my defeat. And if I am not defeated, I do build it. The universe will be forced to choose.”

“What happens if it can’t?”

“Usually? The universe chooses badly.”

A crack of violet light split the air above them. Through it, Mara glimpsed the city folded in on itself, buildings inside buildings, streets twisting into knots. The crack sealed.

Mara stepped closer. “So you’ve made yourself impossible to beat.”

“Impossible to defeat,” Paradox corrected. “Not impossible to persuade.”

He offered her the teacup.

She didn’t take it. “Why do this?”

His smile faded a little. “Because I’ve seen what comes next.”

“And you think freezing everything will stop it?”

“I think I can keep the future from becoming worse.”

“That’s not the same as saving it.”

For the first time, Paradox looked uncertain. The rain hung between them, each drop reflecting a different version of his face: young, old, worried, triumphant.

Mara studied the machine. Its rings spun in opposite directions, each one marked with a date. The center ring bore today’s date—except the final digit was missing.

“Your paradox depends on one thing,” she said. “That you’re defeated by me.”

“Correct.”

“Not that you lose the machine. Not that the machine is destroyed. Just that I defeat you.”

“An elegant distinction.”

“Then you don’t have to be defeated.”

Paradox lifted an eyebrow. “Do go on.”

Mara held out her hand. “Give me the watch.”

He laughed softly. “And why would I do that?”

“Because you’re afraid of the future. I’m afraid of it too. But if you control every second, there’s no future left to save.”

The clocks all clicked once.

Not forward. Not backward. Just once.

Paradox looked down at his pocket watch. Its hands had stopped spinning. For a long moment, the frozen city held its breath.

Then he placed the watch in her palm.

The machine on his back gave a low, shuddering hum. The rings slowed, but they didn’t stop. One by one, the dates blurred into silver lines.

Mara felt the watch grow warm. “What happens now?”

“Now,” said Paradox, “you decide whether to defeat me.”

She closed her fingers around the watch. “No. I decide whether to help you.”

The machine released a pulse of pale light.

The rain fell.

The pigeons resumed their flight. A taxi honked, late for a green light that had been green all along. Around them, the city’s clocks jumped from 4:17 to 4:18.

Paradox looked at the street, then at Mara. “The future is still coming.”

“Good,” she said. “That means we still have time.”

His smile returned—not the smug one, but something smaller and more tired.

“Then I suppose,” he said, “we should make the most of it.”

prompt: A case hinges on something witnessed only by a dead person . To illustrate how ludicrous this is , one side subpoenas the dead person . The dead person shows up and testifies .
content:
### The Witness

The case of Bellwether Pond hinged on a man who had been dead for eleven years.

The pond lay behind a row of cottages and a stand of white pines. For as long as anyone could remember, the people of Bellwether had walked the footpath along its eastern shore. Then a developer bought the cottages, put up a gate, and announced that the path crossed private land.

The town sued.

At trial, the developer’s lawyer argued that the path had never been public. The town’s lawyer produced old maps, old minutes, and a photograph of children carrying fishing poles through the gate that had not yet been built. But the crucial question was where the original boundary stone had stood.

Only one person had seen it moved: Amos Bell, the surveyor.

Amos had died in 2013.

“The town asks you to believe,” said Mr. Quill, the developer’s lawyer, “that the boundary was altered because a man who cannot be questioned supposedly saw it happen. This is not evidence. It is a story.”

The judge adjusted her glasses. “Do you have a point, Mr. Quill?”

“I do, Your Honor.” He turned toward the jury. “If we are to decide this case on the word of a dead man, perhaps we ought to subpoena him.”

The courtroom laughed. Even the judge smiled.

Mr. Quill lifted a folded paper. “In fact, I have.”

The laughter stopped.

He explained that he had filed a subpoena for Amos Bell, addressed to the Bellwether Cemetery, Grave 118. He had done so, he said, to demonstrate the absurdity of the town’s position. The clerk had stamped the document. The sheriff had served it on the cemetery caretaker, who had signed for it.

“Are you telling me you expect the witness to appear?” the judge asked.

“No, Your Honor.”

At 2:17 p.m., the courtroom doors opened.

A thin man in a brown suit stepped inside, carrying a surveyor’s chain over one shoulder. His shoes were muddy. His hair was neatly combed, though a small pine needle clung to his lapel.

“I’m Amos Bell,” he said. “I believe I’ve been summoned.”

The judge stared at him. “Mr. Bell, are you alive?”

“Not since 2013.”

“Can you take an oath?”

“I can tell the truth. I’ve had time to think about it.”

The judge leaned back. “All right. Let’s see where this goes.”

Amos took the stand. The clerk raised the Bible, then hesitated.

“Do I need that?” Amos asked.

“Probably not,” the judge said. “But we’ve started.”

The town’s lawyer, Ms. Saye, approached.

“Mr. Bell, did you see the boundary stone moved?”

“I did.”

“Who moved it?”

“Gideon Vale.” Vale was the developer’s father, long dead himself. “He moved it about twelve feet inland, on a wet Tuesday in October.”

“Why do you remember the date?”

“Because I told him it was a wet Tuesday in October, and he said he’d remember it as the day the town learned to mind its own business.”

Ms. Saye nodded. “Where was the stone before he moved it?”

“Beside the old willow. The path passed between the stone and the water.”

“And afterward?”

“The path was on Vale’s side of the new line.”

The developer’s lawyer stood. “Objection. The witness is dead.”

“Overruled,” said the judge. “I can see that.”

Mr. Quill began his cross-examination.

“Mr. Bell, you expect this jury to believe you can remember a Tuesday from more than twenty years ago?”

“I remember the stone. I remember Mr. Vale. I remember him because he was standing on my measuring chain.”

“Convenient.”

“Not for my chain.”

A few jurors smiled.

“You’re also saying you saw this from a distance?”

“Thirty feet.”

“In the rain?”

“Yes.”

“Through trees?”

“Two trees.”

“After drinking?”

“I had one cup of coffee.”

“Could it have been tea?”

“It could have been terrible coffee.”

Mr. Quill paused. “You admit you don’t remember everything.”

“Of course. I’m dead, not a filing cabinet.”

This time the judge laughed, though she covered it with a cough.

Mr. Quill tried again. “Did you ever tell anyone about this?”

“Many people.”

“Name one.”

“I told the town clerk.”

“She’s dead.”

“Then she can confirm it.”

The jury laughed aloud. The judge rapped her pencil against the bench.

Mr. Quill lowered his voice. “Mr. Bell, you’re aware that your testimony could determine who owns that shoreline?”

“I am.”

“And you have no stake in the outcome?”

Amos looked through the courtroom windows, toward the distant pond.

“I used to fish there,” he said. “I suppose I still do, if the fish don’t mind.”

For a moment, no one spoke.

Then Ms. Saye rose. “Your Honor, the town rests.”

The jury deliberated for three hours. They returned with a verdict for Bellwether: the path was public, and the gate had to come down.

Amos watched them file out.

Mr. Quill approached him in the empty courtroom. “I didn’t think you’d come.”

“Neither did I,” Amos said. “But your subpoena was very clear.”

“Do you plan to appeal?”

“No. I’ve already been called as a witness once. I don’t want to make a habit of it.”

He turned toward the exit. At the doorway, the judge called after him.

“Mr. Bell?”

He looked back.

“Is it really true you can still fish?”

Amos considered this.

“Not legally,” he said, and disappeared into the rain.

content:
In our town, boys could get pregnant. It wasn’t common, but it wasn’t impossible either. Adults talked about it as calmly as they talked about left-handedness.

That didn’t make it feel calm when I stared at the two pink lines on the test.

Maya sat beside me on the bathroom floor, twisting the sleeve of her sweater. “We should tell them,” she said.

“I know.”

“Tonight?”

“I know.”

Neither of us moved.

At dinner, my dad asked how school was. I said, “Fine,” and pushed a pea around my plate. My mom told us about a neighbor’s new puppy. The puppy had chewed a shoe, apparently, and my parents laughed like this was the funniest thing they’d heard all week.

I couldn’t understand how the world could keep being ordinary.

After dinner, I followed them into the living room. Maya came with me, quiet and pale. My parents looked up from the television.

“Can we talk?” I asked.

Dad muted the sound. “Sure. What’s going on?”

My mouth went dry. I’d practiced the words in my room, in the shower, on the bus. They all vanished.

“I’m pregnant,” I said.

For a moment, nobody spoke.

Then Mom stood. “Oh, sweetheart.”

That wasn’t what I’d expected. I’d prepared for anger, disappointment, questions. I hadn’t prepared for her to cross the room and take my hand.

Dad turned off the television. “Are you sure?”

I nodded. “We took two tests.”

Maya looked at the floor. “I’m sorry. We didn’t mean for this to happen.”

“I know,” Mom said gently. She pulled a chair close to mine. “But we need to talk about what happens next. Have you seen a doctor?”

“Not yet.”

“Then we start there,” Dad said. His voice was steady, though his face had gone pale. “We’ll make an appointment tomorrow.”

I stared at him. “You’re not mad?”

“I’m scared,” he said. “That’s different.”

Mom squeezed my hand. “And whatever you decide, you won’t have to figure it out alone.”

The words loosened something in my chest. I leaned forward, and she wrapped her arms around me. I was still terrified. There were questions we hadn’t asked and choices we weren’t ready to make. Tomorrow would bring a doctor, and after that, more hard conversations.

But for the first time since the test turned pink, I wasn’t holding the news by myself.

Maya reached for my other hand. My dad sat down across from us, close enough to be part of the circle.

Outside, the evening carried on—cars passing, a dog barking somewhere down the street, the ordinary world going on.

Inside, my parents stayed with me while it changed.

{prompt}
prompt: You are a child who experienced a nightmare about a werewolf . Now , in every sleep , you experience the same nightmare . You have the choice to claim victory or defeat to end your recurring dream .
content:
**The Last Night of the Werewolf**

The first time I dreamed about the werewolf, I was hiding under my bed.

It was taller than the door and covered in gray fur. Its yellow eyes shone through the dark, and its claws scraped the floor as it searched my room.

I tried to call for Mom, but no sound came out.

Then the werewolf bent down and looked beneath the bed.

I woke up shouting.

Mom came running. She turned on the light, checked the closet, and sat beside me until my hands stopped shaking. “It was only a dream,” she said.

But the next night, it came back.

And the night after that.

Every time, I hid beneath the bed. Every time, the werewolf found me. And every time, I woke before it could reach me—though I still felt its hot breath on my face.

After a while, I started dreading bedtime. I tried leaving the lamp on. I tried sleeping with the blanket over my head. I even asked Dad if we could get a dog to guard my room. None of it helped.

Then, one night, the dream changed.

I was back in my room, crouched beneath the bed. The familiar claws scraped across the floor.

But this time, a voice spoke inside my head.

*You can end this now.*

I peered through the dust and saw the werewolf waiting beside my bed.

*Choose,* said the voice. *Victory or defeat.*

My knees trembled. I could run, but I knew where that would lead. I could let the werewolf win. I imagined its claws reaching for me, and my heart pounded so hard I thought the dream might hear it.

Then I remembered something Mom had said: “Being brave doesn’t mean you aren’t scared. It means you try, even while you are.”

I crawled out from under the bed.

The werewolf bared its teeth. I was still frightened, but I stood as tall as I could.

“I choose victory,” I said.

My voice was small, but the werewolf stopped.

I looked closer. Its yellow eyes weren’t angry. They were sad.

“You don’t have to chase me,” I told it.

The werewolf lowered its head. For a moment, neither of us moved. Then the fur along its shoulders began to fade, like mist in sunlight. Its claws became fingers. Its sharp teeth became an ordinary, crooked smile.

The creature was no longer a werewolf. It was just a lonely old wolf, no bigger than our family dog.

It gave a soft huff and vanished.

I woke up in my own bed, with the lamp glowing beside me. My heart was beating fast, but I wasn’t shouting. I wasn’t hiding.

The next night, I dreamed of the forest again. But there was no werewolf waiting in the dark. Only moonlight on the trees, and a small gray wolf walking beside me.

I never had that nightmare again.

Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: You wait tables in a Southern bar with a cartoonishly sassy , gay , black cook and are best friends with his sister . A vampire walks in to have a drink of the new fake blood your bar sells . You can also hear people 's thoughts and you 're half human , half fairy . Who killed your grandmother ?
content:
The first thing I heard from the vampire was, *Please let this taste less like pennies than the last one.*

The second was, *Don’t look at the mirror.*

He came in just before midnight, when the cicadas outside the Bluebird Lounge were loud enough to drown out ordinary sins. He wore a charcoal suit and carried an umbrella, though the sky was clear. His skin had the pale, translucent look of something kept too long in a cellar.

I set a glass of our new house special on the bar: **FAKE BLOOD—CHERRY, IRON, OR O NEGATIVE.**

“On the house,” I said. “We’re trying to win your kind over.”

He glanced at the label. “My kind?”

“People who enjoy a beverage with a warning on it.”

From the kitchen, Leon called, “Tell him if he hates it, he can take it up with the supplier. I’m not squeezing more cherries for anybody.”

Leon was my best friend’s older brother, a cook, and the only man I knew who could make a Sunday special sound like a personal favor. He was Black, gay, and sharp enough to peel paint with a sentence. He was also kind, though he preferred to keep that fact hidden beneath three layers of sarcasm.

His sister, June, and I had been best friends since we were eight and both got caught stealing peaches from my grandmother’s orchard. June said we’d been bonded by crime. Grandma said we’d been bonded by poor judgment.

Grandma had been dead for six months.

The sheriff called it a fall down the cellar stairs. I heard the lie in his thoughts at the funeral, clear as a bell: *She should’ve stayed out of it.*

I’d spent every day since trying to work out what *it* was.

The vampire took a sip. His mind made a small, unhappy noise.

“Well?” I asked.

“It tastes like someone described blood to a person who has never met a tomato.”

“I’ll tell the supplier.”

“Don’t. I’m sure they’re doing their best.”

He looked at me then—not at my face, exactly, but at the faint gold shimmer around my ears that human eyes didn’t notice. I tucked my hair forward. Half human, half fairy, I’d inherited my grandmother’s pointed ears, her knack for hearing thoughts, and none of her talent for keeping out of other people’s business.

The vampire’s thoughts went quiet.

That was unusual. Most people’s minds rattled away around me like loose silverware. His was a locked room.

“What brings you to the Bluebird?” I asked.

“Thirst.”

“Besides the obvious.”

He turned the glass between his fingers. “I knew your grandmother.”

I dropped the towel I was holding.

In the kitchen, a pan clanged. Leon appeared in the doorway, wiping his hands on his apron. “You knew Hazel?”

The vampire nodded. “She helped me once.”

“When?” I asked.

“Thirty years ago.”

“That doesn’t explain why you’re here now.”

“No,” he said. “It doesn’t.”

June came out of the office, where she’d been counting receipts. She took one look at my face and slid beside me. “What’s going on?”

The vampire’s eyes moved to her. “Your grandmother was murdered.”

The bar seemed to shrink around us. Even the jukebox went quiet between songs.

“I know,” I said. “Who did it?”

“I don’t.”

“Then why come here?”

He finally drank again. His thoughts opened a crack, and through it I heard something old and cold: *The sheriff was there. The cellar door. The silver knife.*

I caught my breath.

“Sheriff Bell,” I said.

Leon’s expression changed. The joke left his face. “You sure?”

“I heard—”

The vampire set down his glass. “I saw him leave her house that night. I didn’t know she was dead until much later.”

“You saw him and said nothing?” June demanded.

“I was afraid.”

“Of the sheriff?”

“Of what he would tell the town I was.”

The Bluebird’s back door banged open. Sheriff Bell stepped inside, hat in hand, smiling the way men smile when they’ve decided the room belongs to them.

“Evening,” he said. His thoughts were loud as a dropped tray: *The vampire. The girl. Loose ends.*

My stomach tightened. The fairy part of me stirred, bright and furious.

Bell rested one hand on the bar. “You folks having a meeting?”

“Just discussing my grandmother,” I said.

His smile slipped.

Leon leaned on the kitchen doorway. “That’s a strange subject to bring up at a bar.”

“Not if you’re the one who killed her,” June said.

Bell laughed. *She doesn’t know,* his mind said. *She can’t prove it.*

I looked at the vampire. “Did you see what he carried?”

“A knife,” he said. “Silver-handled.”

Bell’s right hand twitched toward his belt.

And then I heard the second thought beneath the first, the one he’d buried so deep it had grown teeth: *Hazel said she’d tell them about the orchard. About the names.*

Grandma’s orchard. The place where the old fairy boundary ran through the roots. The place where she’d found Bell digging up the stones that kept the boundary sealed.

I knew then what she’d died protecting.

I also knew what Bell feared most.

“Everybody in town can hear about the orchard by morning,” I said. “Unless you’d like to explain why you were digging there.”

Bell stared at me. His mind flared with panic, then went blank.

Leon stepped forward, holding a cast-iron skillet. “And before you consider doing anything foolish, Sheriff, remember I’ve been working with this thing all night.”

June reached for my hand.

Bell looked from the skillet to the vampire, then to the three people who had stopped being afraid of him.

At last, he backed toward the door.

Outside, the cicadas began again.

The vampire picked up his glass. “I should have come sooner.”

“Yes,” I said. “You should have.”

He swallowed the last of the fake blood and made a face. “Still tastes like pennies.”

From the kitchen, Leon called, “Then stop drinking pennies, Count Blah-blah.”

June squeezed my hand. For the first time in six months, Grandma’s thoughts weren’t the loudest thing in my head.

For the first time, there was room to hear my own.

{prompt}
prompt: As you tend your large garden , you notice a naked couple walk unnervingly close to a tree bearing golden fruit ...
content:
Every morning, I walked the garden before the sun had fully climbed over the wall.

It was too large for one person, really—six acres of roses, herbs, orchards, and winding paths, all inherited from a great-aunt who had left me the keys and no explanation. I liked the work. The pruning, the weeding, the steady conversation of birds. A garden asks for patience and doesn’t mind if you answer in silence.

That morning, the silence felt different.

I was tying up a drooping pear branch when I saw them near the far orchard: a man and a woman, both naked, walking hand in hand beneath the trees.

I froze.

They were young, though not young enough to seem like children. Their skin shone with dew. They moved without hurry, without embarrassment, and without looking around—as if they had never learned that anyone else might be watching.

“Excuse me,” I called.

They didn’t turn.

I followed at a distance, my pruning shears still in one hand. The couple passed the apple trees, then the old stone fountain. They were heading toward the garden’s heart, where the golden tree stood.

It had been there longer than the house. Its trunk was pale as bone, its leaves dark green and glossy. In summer, it bore one fruit: a perfect golden pear, warm to the touch even in winter. My great-aunt had warned me never to pick it.

“Some things,” she’d said, “are safest when they remain wanted.”

The couple stopped beneath it.

The woman lifted her face toward the fruit. The man’s hand tightened around hers.

“Don’t,” I said.

At last, they looked back.

Their eyes were identical: clear, gray, and full of a terrible sadness.

“Is it ripe?” the woman asked.

“It’s not for you.”

“Who is it for?” said the man.

I had no answer. I’d spent years tending that tree, guarding it from birds and storms, and never once asked what the fruit was for.

The woman reached up. Her fingers brushed the lowest leaf.

The garden shuddered.

Every fountain went still. Birds fell silent in the branches. From somewhere beyond the orchard came the slow creak of a gate opening.

I stepped between them and the tree.

“You can’t have it,” I said, though my voice had gone thin.

The man studied me. “You’ve been keeping it for us.”

“No.”

“You’ve been keeping it from us,” said the woman.

The words struck deeper than they should have. I thought of my great-aunt’s locked rooms, her unfinished letters, the way she had put the garden in my care without ever explaining why.

The fruit gleamed above us, bright as a small captured sun.

“Take it,” the woman said, looking at me now. “You’re the one who’s hungry.”

I was.

Not for food. For the truth of the house, the reason for the garden, the faces that appeared in my dreams: a woman laughing beneath a white tree, a man standing at a gate with soil on his hands.

I reached up.

The fruit came free with a soft, almost apologetic snap.

At once, the couple vanished.

The gate beyond the orchard slammed shut. The birds began again. A breeze crossed the grass, and the golden tree shivered, bare-branched.

In my palm, the fruit was no longer golden. It was an ordinary pear, small and green, with a bite taken from its side.

I carried it to the house and set it on the kitchen table.

Then I opened the drawer where my great-aunt had kept her letters. At the very bottom lay an envelope with my name on it. Inside was a single sentence, written in her wavering hand:

*When they come back, let them leave hungry.*

I looked out at the orchard.

Beyond the wall, someone was knocking.

prompt: Fear and The Emotions of Social Interaction ( Come Together )
content:
## The Space Between Hellos

Mara arrived twelve minutes early and still felt late.

Through the community hall’s glass doors, she could see people gathering beneath strings of paper lanterns. They stood in loose circles, holding cups and laughing as if laughter were something they had brought from home. Mara stayed on the pavement, one hand gripping the strap of her bag.

“You can still leave,” said Fear.

Fear always spoke in Mara’s own voice, only clearer.

“I know,” Mara whispered.

Inside, someone dropped a spoon. The small clatter made the room burst into laughter. Mara’s stomach tightened. She imagined stepping in, saying the wrong thing, standing alone while everyone noticed she was alone.

Then another voice stirred—Quieter than Fear, but no less hers.

“You could also stay.”

Mara looked down at the invitation folded in her coat pocket. The gathering was for the neighbors who had helped after her father died. She had meant to thank them. She had practiced a sentence in the mirror, but every version sounded either too formal or too close to crying.

A woman near the door spotted her. It was June, who lived upstairs and had once left a casserole on Mara’s doorstep without asking for anything in return.

“There you are,” June said, opening the door. “I’m glad you came.”

Fear stepped forward. “Tell her you have a headache.”

But Warmth, shy and unfamiliar, touched Mara’s shoulder. “She means it.”

“I’m glad too,” Mara said. It came out smaller than she wanted, but June smiled as if she’d heard every word.

Inside, the hall was louder than it had looked from the pavement. Someone asked Mara how she was. Someone else asked whether she wanted tea. A man she didn’t recognize told a story about her father insisting on fixing a broken fence in the rain. Mara laughed, then surprised herself by crying.

The room quieted. For one frightening second, she felt every face turn toward her.

Fear said, “Now they’ll remember this.”

But June passed her a napkin. The man who had told the story lowered his eyes, giving her privacy. Across the room, someone raised a cup—not to silence her, but to make room for her grief.

Mara understood then that fear had not lied about the risk. She might stumble. She might cry. People might see her.

Fear simply hadn’t mentioned what else could happen.

She could be welcomed. She could be remembered alongside others. She could say, “Thank you for taking care of him,” and let the sentence be imperfect.

So she did.

The words trembled on their way out. They were met by nods, a hand resting gently on her arm, and several voices saying, “Of course.”

Fear stayed beside her through the rest of the evening. So did sadness. But Joy appeared, too, first as a laugh at the tea table, then as the warm ache of hearing her father’s name spoken kindly.

When Mara left, she was still tired. She was still nervous about the next gathering.

But outside, under the lanterns, she no longer felt alone.

All her feelings had come with her. None had needed to disappear for her to belong.

prompt: You find a maintenance hatch to Earth .
content:
The hatch was behind the water recycler, where no hatch had any business being.

You found it while looking for the leak. The recycler had been coughing up rust-colored water for three days, and the manual said to check the intake valve. You pulled away a panel, reached into the warm dark, and touched a wheel of cold metal.

There was no label. Just a small circle stamped into the wheel: a blue world, clouded in white.

You turned it.

The hatch sighed open.

On the other side was rain.

Not a recording. Not a projection. Rain ran down a narrow shaft cut through black stone, pattering on a ledge inches beyond the hatch. You smelled wet dirt, leaves, and something sharp and green that made your eyes sting.

Earth, the maintenance logs called it. A closed system. Uninhabitable. No surface access authorized.

You had been born aboard the ship. You had seen Earth in lessons: a blue globe under glass, its oceans labeled with names no one used anymore. Your grandparents had told stories about it, but the stories didn’t agree. There were beaches, deserts, forests, cities buried under forests. There were birds that sang at dawn and storms that swallowed towns.

You put one hand on the stone ledge.

The ship’s alarm began to pulse behind you. “Unscheduled pressure loss,” said the calm voice in the ceiling. “Please return to your assigned section.”

You should have closed the hatch.

Instead, you climbed through.

The shaft opened onto a hillside beneath a gray sky. Rain soaked your uniform in seconds. Below, a valley rolled away beneath a tangle of young trees. Their branches bent in the wind. Beyond them, a river flashed silver.

You laughed. The sound came out too loud, too small, and the rain took it.

Then you noticed the maintenance tags.

They were fixed to the trees in neat rows, old metal plaques stamped with dates. The earliest was from the year the ship had left orbit. The latest was only eleven months old.

Earth was not abandoned.

It was being repaired.

A figure stood at the edge of the river, wearing a patched yellow coat. They raised one hand. You raised yours.

Behind you, the hatch began to close. The ship was calling you back—not with an alarm now, but with your own name, spoken in the voice of your mother, who had died before you were old enough to remember her.

You stepped toward the figure.

The hatch shut with a soft, final click.

For the first time in your life, the ground moved beneath your feet. Somewhere overhead, rain slid from the leaves, and Earth kept turning.

prompt: - A successful movie actor decides to go through and watch his older films . But , while watching , discovers odd things . Scenes he does n't remember , lines that were n't in the script , and interviews he never did . It 's in all his movies , and gets steadily more sinister .
content:
## The Unremembered Scene

At fifty-eight, Daniel Vale decided to watch all his films in order.

It was his wife’s idea, though she’d meant it as a joke. They were sorting through boxes in the attic when she found a stack of old reviews and said, “You should watch them all. See whether you’ve gotten better.”

Daniel had laughed. Then he’d thought about it.

There were forty-three films, not counting cameos. He rented a screening room at the studio and asked his assistant to make a list. He started with *The Orchard*, the little black-and-white drama that had made his name.

The first odd thing happened eleven minutes in.

Daniel’s character, a young man named Peter, was standing in a kitchen with his mother. Daniel remembered the scene. They argued about money. She asked him to stay. He left.

But in the version on the screen, Peter didn’t leave.

He turned back from the door and said, “You can stop waiting now.”

His mother looked at him, suddenly frightened. Then the scene cut to the next one.

Daniel leaned forward.

He rewound it. The line was still there.

He called up the shooting script on his tablet. No such line. He checked the scene in the original screenplay. No kitchen argument at all. The footage looked clean—no jump, no splice, no different film stock. Just Daniel, younger by thirty years, saying something he had no memory of saying.

“Probably an alternate take,” he told himself.

He watched the rest of the film.

In the last scene, Peter stood in a field as the wind moved through the grass. Daniel remembered the shot: Peter alone, looking toward the horizon.

Now there was a boy in the distance, dressed in a red coat. He stood perfectly still, facing the camera.

Daniel checked the credits. No boy.

He went home and told his wife about the extra scene. She shrugged. “Could be a restoration mistake.”

“Could be.”

He didn’t mention the boy.

The next film was a thriller he’d made five years later. This time, the strange moment came during a police interrogation. Daniel’s character sat beneath a harsh light and denied knowing anything about a murder.

The detective leaned across the table.

“You heard him after you left,” she said.

Daniel felt the room go cold.

He knew the scene. He’d shot it in one take. The detective’s line, according to the script, was *You saw him that night.*

He watched it again. *You heard him after you left.*

In the next film, a comedy, a waitress passed Daniel’s character in a restaurant and murmured, “You said you’d come back.”

In a western, a dying outlaw gripped his hand and whispered, “How many times do we have to do this?”

Different films. Different crews. Different studios. The same sensation: a word placed carefully where it did not belong.

And, somewhere in each one, the boy in the red coat.

Sometimes he was at the edge of the frame. Sometimes behind a crowd. Once, in a romantic drama, he sat alone at a bus stop while Daniel kissed his leading lady beneath a streetlamp.

Daniel began watching with the lights on.

By the time he reached *The North Line*, he had stopped taking notes. He sat with his hands clasped between his knees and watched himself play a man lost in the Arctic.

In the final act, Daniel’s character stumbled into an empty cabin. He was supposed to find a map on the table. Instead, he found a small red mitten.

He picked it up.

The camera moved closer to his face. His eyes filled with tears. He said, “I looked for you.”

Daniel stood so quickly his chair toppled behind him.

He had never been told to cry in that scene. He remembered the map. He remembered shooting it three times because the prop kept sliding off the table. He remembered the director laughing about it.

He did not remember a mitten.

He left without finishing the film.

For two days, he tried to find an explanation. He called the studio archivist, who blamed a corrupted master. He called his agent, who suggested he was exhausted. His wife asked him to take a break.

Then a package arrived at the house.

It contained a DVD and a printed transcript of a television interview. The DVD was labeled *DANIEL VALE — THE LATE SHOW, 2002*.

Daniel watched it alone.

The interview set was unfamiliar. The host was a woman with dark hair and an expression of patient concern. Daniel remembered doing dozens of interviews that year, but not this one. He couldn’t recall her name. He couldn’t recall the studio.

On-screen, the woman asked him about his preparation for *The North Line*.

“Was it difficult spending so much time alone?” she asked.

Daniel gave a practiced smile. “Not really. I’m comfortable with my own company.”

The woman glanced down at her cards.

“Did you hear him after you left?”

The smile faded from Daniel’s face.

For a moment, the Daniel on-screen stared past the camera. Then he said, “Every night, until I stopped answering.”

The interview ended.

Daniel took the DVD to his office and searched the internet. No listing. No mention in databases. No photographs. The transcript was unsigned and undated, except for the year printed at the top.

He called his assistant.

“Did you send me this?”

“No.”

“Did anyone?”

There was a pause. “It came through the mail?”

“Yes.”

“From where?”

The return address was the studio archive.

The next morning, Daniel went there himself.

The archivist, a thin man named Morris, showed him the records for the interview. There were none.

“Maybe it was a test tape,” Morris said. “Something assembled for internal use.”

“By whom?”

Morris looked at the screen. “I don’t know.”

“Can you check the source?”

“I can try.”

Daniel took the DVD back. He was leaving when Morris called after him.

“Mr. Vale?”

Daniel turned.

Morris looked uneasy. “There’s something else.”

He brought up a clip from the interview on his monitor. The image was grainy now, the woman’s face blurred by lines of digital noise. Daniel heard his younger self say, *Every night, until I stopped answering.*

Then the woman leaned toward the camera.

“You should let him out,” she said.

Morris froze.

The clip ended.

“That wasn’t there before,” Daniel said.

“I know.”

That evening, Daniel returned to the screening room.

He had one film left: *The Glass House*, his most recent, shot only six months earlier. He had chosen it because he remembered every day of production. There had been no strange boy on set. No unscripted lines. No missing scenes.

He watched the first hour without interruption.

Then came the final scene.

Daniel’s character, a retired architect, sat alone in a darkened theater. The film’s ending was meant to be quiet: he listened to an old recording of his late wife and watched dust drift in the projector beam.

But on-screen, Daniel’s character lowered the recording and looked over his shoulder.

There was no one behind him.

He looked back at the camera.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

Daniel’s mouth went dry.

The character continued, “I didn’t know how long you’d been waiting.”

The film cut to black.

Daniel reached for the remote. Before he could press stop, the sound of a child’s voice came through the speakers.

“Open the door.”

The picture returned.

The theater on-screen was empty, except for a single red coat draped over the back of the seat directly behind the camera.

Daniel stood. The screen went dark.

From somewhere behind him came the soft scrape of a shoe against carpet.

He turned.

There was no one in the screening room. Only the rows of empty seats and the faint green glow of the exit sign.

His phone rang. His wife.

“Are you still at the studio?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“Daniel, I got a call from someone asking for you.”

“Who?”

“I don’t know. A boy, I think. He said you were supposed to come back.”

Daniel stared at the dark screen.

“Did he leave a number?”

“No. He just said you’d know where.”

The call ended.

In the silence, Daniel heard the projector motor start up behind him.

He faced the screen.

It lit with a picture he had never seen before: a little boy in a red coat standing in the aisle of a small, old theater. The image was grainy, almost black and white. The boy lifted his face to the camera.

Daniel felt the memory arrive—not as a thought, but as a door opening.

A narrow aisle. A dark theater. His own small hand slipping from someone else’s. The smell of dust and hot metal.

And a voice, behind him, saying, *Wait here.*

The boy on-screen looked toward the empty seat beside him.

Then he said, “You took so long.”

Daniel didn’t move.

The screen flickered. The boy turned away and began walking down the aisle, toward the back of the theater.

The exit sign above the real door buzzed softly.

Daniel watched the boy disappear into the dark. Then, from somewhere beyond the screen, came the sound of a door opening.

prompt: You wake up in a pile of hay , you are the infamous Wizard of the Beer .
content:
You wake up in a pile of hay with a chicken standing on your chest.

It regards you with the calm disappointment of a judge.

“Off,” you croak.

The chicken hops down. Your head throbs. Your robes smell like smoke, hops, and something that might once have been a cheese. A crooked wooden staff lies beside you, its brass tip shaped like a tiny foaming mug.

Then you notice the villagers staring through the barn door.

One of them whispers, “It’s him.”

Another crosses herself. “The Wizard of the Beer.”

You sit up too quickly and the world tilts. “I’m sorry—who?”

“The infamous Wizard of the Beer,” says a little girl, with the reverence usually reserved for dragons. “You turned the king’s river into ale.”

“I did what?”

“Three kings ago,” says an old farmer. “The river ran amber for a week. Fine drinking, terrible fishing.”

You look at the staff. A name is carved into its handle: **B. WIZARD**. Beneath it, in smaller letters: **RETURN TO THE BREWERY WHEN SOBER**.

A memory flickers: moonlight on copper kettles. A spell spoken backward. A man in a crown shouting, “Make it stop bubbling!”

Then nothing.

The villagers crowd closer. Their mayor holds out a wooden tankard. “Our well has gone dry. Can you help?”

You stand, brushing hay from your robes. “I’m an infamous wizard, apparently. I must be able to do something.”

You raise the staff.

The brass mug glows. A warm breeze slips through the barn, carrying the scent of fresh bread and rain. Somewhere beneath the village, water stirs. The ground gives a soft, friendly gurgle.

At the well, a clear stream bursts upward—not ale, not magic, just clean, cold water. The villagers cheer. The little girl fills her tankard and takes a sip.

“Disappointing,” she says.

“Good,” you reply. “Water’s underrated.”

The mayor squints at you. “So you’re retired?”

You look at the chicken, now perched on your staff. You look at the distant hills, where a plume of green smoke curls above what might be a brewery—or a very confused dragon.

“I think,” you say, “I’m going to find out what I did.”

The chicken clucks.

“And after that,” you add, “perhaps a small beer.”

The villagers cheer again. This time, you’re fairly sure they’re cheering for the beer.
