{prompt}
prompt: You arrive in the year 1000 , and all you have are the clothes on your back , a laptop with the entire Wikipedia library , and a solar charger .
content:
## The Book of the Sun

The first thing I learned about the year 1000 was that it smelled like wet wool.

The second was that no one understood me.

I came to in a field beneath a gray Icelandic sky, wearing jeans, a sweatshirt, and shoes already sinking into the mud. My laptop was under one arm. The folded solar charger was in my backpack. Beyond a low stone wall, a girl watched me with the solemn suspicion of a cat.

I tried English. She tried Norse. We made no progress.

Then she pointed at the laptop.

When I opened it, she ran.

By dusk, the whole farm had gathered around me. The farmer held a knife. His wife held a baby. The girl—whose name, I eventually learned, was Astrid—stood behind them, peering at the screen.

I showed them a picture of the moon.

They leaned closer.

I showed them the Earth, blue and white against black. The farmer crossed himself, though I would not learn the word for that for months. Astrid didn’t look afraid. She looked annoyed that I had brought her something astonishing without explaining it.

The laptop had a full charge. It had every article in Wikipedia, downloaded and searchable, but no internet, no charger that fit any socket in the world, and no way to make anyone understand its words. I had a solar panel, which seemed less like technology than a promise: if the sun came back, the machine might live.

I began with pictures. A cow. A fish. A map. A drawing of a hand.

Astrid learned the word “hand” first. I learned her name second.

Weeks passed. I traded labor for food, and awkward gestures for words. I mucked out stalls, carried water, and tried not to stare at the smoke-blackened rafters. In return, Astrid taught me Norse by pointing at things and laughing when I got them wrong.

The laptop became our third teacher. I found articles with illustrations and showed them one image at a time. They were fascinated by maps, especially the one of the world. Astrid would tap the screen and ask the names of places. I could only answer with my own language, then point, then try again.

Winter darkened the days. I used the laptop sparingly. By then I could read a little, though the words on the screen were still strange and stiff beside the speech around me. I learned to search for things I could explain with drawings: stars, ships, plants, the human body.

Then Astrid’s little brother cut his foot on a broken iron tool.

It was a small wound. It became a bad one.

His mother washed it with water. The farmer wrapped it in a cloth. I opened the laptop and searched for wound care, but the article might as well have been written in the language of angels. I tried to remember what I could. Clean water. Clean hands. Fresh cloth. Don’t seal dirt inside. I boiled water in a pot and asked Astrid to translate as best she could.

They watched me as if I were choosing between spells.

The boy’s fever rose that night. I sat beside him, helpless, while the fire snapped in the hearth. At dawn, the fever broke. By the end of the week, he was sitting up, furious that everyone was still fussing over him.

Astrid told people I had healed him.

I told her I hadn’t. She frowned, then said something I understood as: “You helped.”

After that, the farmer let me keep the laptop in the best-lit corner of the house. When spring returned, I unfolded the solar panel on the roof and caught the long, pale sunlight. The battery crept back to life.

I began to make a book.

Not from the laptop itself; there was too much, and I could not translate most of it. I drew pictures and dictated simple things to Astrid, who wrote them down in the letters she was learning. How to boil water. How to keep a clean cloth for a wound. How the moon went around the Earth—or, at least, how the picture showed it. How far away the stars were. Which plants in the fields were safe to eat, checked against the local knowledge of people who knew the land far better than I ever would.

The book grew slowly. It was not Wikipedia. It was a few scraps of what I could carry across the gap between us.

One summer, word came from the south that people were gathering at the Alþingi to settle a great argument about gods and laws. Astrid asked if the laptop could tell us what decision they would make.

I searched the history of Iceland. I found the answer.

Then I closed the computer.

“What does it say?” she asked.

“That I know what happened,” I said, choosing words she would understand. “Not what should happen.”

She considered this. “Those are different?”

“Yes.”

She nodded, though I wasn’t sure she believed me.

Years later—though I couldn’t say how many—the laptop’s battery began to fail. The screen flickered. The solar charger still worked, but less and less seemed to enter the machine. I had hoped the encyclopedia would be a bridge. Instead, it had become a box of fading light.

Astrid was grown by then. Her brother had children of his own. She sat beside me as the screen dimmed, and I showed her the Earth once more: a bright sphere, floating in darkness.

“Is that all the world?” she asked.

“All of it.”

“And all the knowledge?”

“No.” I smiled. “Only what people wrote down.”

She thought about this, then handed me a fresh sheet of parchment. Outside, the sun shone low over the hills.

“Then we should write more,” she said.

The laptop went dark before evening. But the book did not. It passed from hand to hand, changing as it went—some drawings corrected, some pages added, some things I had gotten wrong crossed out by people who knew better.

By the time the last of my borrowed words had failed me, I understood what Astrid had understood from the beginning.

A machine could hold a library.

Only people could make it matter.

“Hmm, kitten…”

Mara paused in the doorway. A tiny gray cat sat in the middle of her kitchen table, surrounded by the evidence of a crime: one overturned flour jar, three paw prints, and a half-eaten cinnamon bun.

The kitten looked up at her with enormous green eyes.

“Hmm, kitten,” Mara repeated. “How did you even get up there?”

The kitten gave a squeaky meow.

Mara set down her groceries. “And where’s your mother?”

At that, the kitten sprang off the table and raced down the hall. Mara followed, stepping over a trail of flour that led to the little gap beneath the back door. Outside, rain pattered against the windows. A striped cat sat on the porch, soaked and shivering.

Mara opened the door. The mother cat darted inside, scooped up her kitten by the scruff, then stopped to look back.

“You can stay,” Mara said. “Both of you. But the cinnamon buns are off-limits.”

The kitten mewed.

“Don’t argue,” Mara said, though she was already smiling.

By morning, the rain had stopped. The kitten slept in a basket by the stove, and its mother curled beside it. On the kitchen table sat a fresh cinnamon bun, untouched.

Mara narrowed her eyes.

The kitten opened one green eye.

“Hmm,” Mara said. “I’ll be watching you.”

prompt: The Earth is made of memory foam and humans have developed a nomadic lifestyle to keep from sinking too far in .
content:
## The Long Exhale

By the time Tavi was born, the road behind her family had already begun to rise.

It lifted slowly, the way a mattress swells after someone gets up. Their footprints softened. Wheel ruts eased shut. Even the shallow hollow where Tavi’s grandmother had once slept—before Tavi was born, before her mother was born—had nearly vanished.

“Nothing lasts,” Grandmother Sella liked to say.

Then she would tap the ground with her walking stick.

“Except what takes its time.”

The Earth took its time with everything. A person who stood too long sank ankle-deep. A house left in one place for a season settled to its windows. The oldest stories told of people who had tried to stay put: whole towns pressed into the ground, their rooftops eventually level with the fields.

So people traveled.

Tavi’s family moved with the herds, the weather, and the great slow sigh of the land. They slept on wide, flexible platforms that spread their weight. They wore broad-bottomed boots. Even their songs were made for walking: verses long enough to carry a caravan over the softest miles.

Tavi loved the road. She loved waking to a new horizon, and the way familiar hills changed shape as the foam beneath them slowly recovered. She loved that, if she looked back far enough, she could see where they had been.

But she hated how slowly Grandmother Sella walked.

“We should stop,” Tavi said one morning, when Sella stumbled for the third time.

Her mother glanced toward the horizon. “We’ll stop at the next firm ridge.”

“And if there isn’t one?”

“Then we keep going.”

Sella smiled at Tavi. “That’s the whole wisdom of it.”

By noon, the caravan reached a wide valley. The ground there was soft as bread dough, but the wind had combed it smooth. Beyond it, the mountains sat low and blue.

Tavi’s mother said they should cross before dusk.

Sella sat down.

Not a quick rest, the kind the caravan allowed between songs. She lowered herself onto the ground and folded her hands in her lap.

“I’m tired,” she said.

Tavi looked at her mother. Her mother looked at the valley.

The caravan shifted uneasily. They had stopped on soft ground. Everyone knew what happened when too much weight gathered in one place.

“We can make a platform,” Tavi said.

“We don’t have enough,” her mother replied.

Tavi looked at the wagons, the bedrolls, the broad sheets of canvas folded along the pack animals’ sides. She looked at the people standing in a loose ring around Sella, each one pressing the earth deeper.

“Then we share what we have.”

She ran to the nearest wagon. The others followed, though they were frightened. They laid out canvas and lashed the wagon poles into a broad frame. They slid it beneath Sella, then spread the other platforms around it, linking them edge to edge.

The ground dipped as they worked. It pulled at their boots. One of the pack animals sank to its knees, and three people strained to lift it free.

“Don’t gather there!” Tavi shouted. “Spread out!”

They obeyed, stepping onto the canvas, the frames, the wagon beds. The weight of the caravan widened across the valley like a hand opening.

When the sun touched the mountains, they had built a small island on the Earth.

Sella lay beneath a blanket, with Tavi beside her. The caravan crowded the platforms, but no one sank. Around them, the valley held their shape: a broad, shallow bowl.

“Listen,” Sella whispered.

At first Tavi heard only the wind. Then she heard a faint creaking, deep beneath the ground, as if the whole world were settling into sleep.

“Is the Earth remembering us?” Tavi asked.

Sella closed her eyes. “It remembers everyone.”

They stayed through the night. Sella died just before dawn, while the sky was still pale.

In the morning, the caravan prepared to move. They lifted the platforms and packed the poles. Tavi stood at the valley’s edge and looked back. Their shapes remained pressed into the foam: a circle of beds and wagons, the outline of a woman lying at its center.

“Will it stay?” she asked.

“For a while,” said her mother.

Tavi knew what that meant. The Earth would slowly rise. The valley would smooth. One day, even Sella’s hollow would be gone.

She took her first step toward the next ridge.

Behind her, the ground began its long exhale.

prompt: Mission Compromised ! ABORT ! ABORT !
content:
### The Abort Signal

“Mission compromised. Abort. Abort.”

The warning filled Mara Venn’s helmet, calm and metallic.

Beyond the cracked visor of the shuttle, the research station turned slowly above the blue curve of Earth. One solar wing was gone. The other flashed in and out of sunlight like a dying eye.

Mara checked the signal. “Control, repeat.”

“Mission compromised. Abort. Abort.” Then silence.

Her copilot, Jin, leaned over the console. “That wasn’t Control.”

“No.” Mara looked at the station’s dark airlock. “It came from inside.”

Their mission was simple: dock, recover the station’s flight recorder, and return. The crew had evacuated six months earlier, after an electrical fire. Nothing alive was supposed to remain.

Jin’s fingers hovered over the controls. “We should go.”

A knock sounded through the shuttle’s hull.

Once.

Twice.

Then came a voice over the short-range channel, thin with static.

“Please,” it said. “I’m still here.”

Mara stared at the airlock.

“Could be a recording,” Jin said.

“Could be.”

The voice came again. “Commander Venn?”

That was Mara’s name.

The station’s exterior cameras were dead. Its power readings were nearly zero. Docking would mean entering a structure that might not hold pressure—and if the warning was real, the shuttle’s automated systems had already judged the mission too dangerous.

“Control,” Mara said, “we have a possible survivor.”

No reply.

Jin shook his head. “The order was clear.”

“So was the voice.”

“Mara, if we open that hatch and the station’s breached—”

“I know.”

She keyed the manual override. The shuttle’s computer protested. A red warning bloomed across her display:

**MISSION COMPROMISED. ABORT. ABORT.**

Mara pressed through it.

The airlock took seven minutes to cycle. Each one seemed longer than the last. When the inner hatch finally opened, Mara stepped into the station with a tether clipped to her suit.

The corridor was dark except for the glow of emergency strips. A drift of papers turned slowly in the air. At the far end, something tapped against a sealed laboratory door.

Mara reached it and found a child’s hand pressed to the small window.

Not a child, she realized. A young technician—barely twenty—floating inside a pressure-safe room, pale and exhausted. He held up a sign against the glass.

**I CAN’T OPEN IT FROM HERE.**

Mara’s suit radio crackled.

“Mission compromised,” said the station computer. “Unauthorized personnel aboard. Abort.”

The young man shook his head and pointed behind him.

On the lab wall, someone had written in marker:

**THE RECORDER IS LYING.**

Mara looked at the technician.

“What happened?”

He mouthed something through the glass. She couldn’t hear him.

She pressed her helmet to the window.

“The fire,” he said. “It wasn’t an accident.”

The station computer repeated its warning.

“Mission compromised. Abort. Abort.”

Mara looked back toward the shuttle. Earth turned beyond the broken station, bright and distant.

Then she pulled the emergency release.

The lock disengaged. The door opened.

“Jin,” she said over comms, “we’re bringing someone home.”

For a moment, there was only static.

Then Jin answered, “Copy.”

Behind them, the station’s warning continued to echo through the dark.

This time, Mara understood it differently.

The mission wasn’t compromised because they had found a survivor.

It was compromised because someone had tried to make sure they wouldn’t.

prompt: As a joke , you decide to run for president under two tickets simultaneously : one as a Republican and one as a Democrat . 3 months before nomination , you are the frontrunner for both parties .
content:
The joke began at a diner.

“Honestly,” I said, stirring my coffee, “I could run for president as a Republican and a Democrat at the same time.”

My sister looked up from her pancakes. “You can’t do that.”

“Not with that attitude.”

By noon, I’d registered two campaign websites. By Friday, I had two campaign offices: one in a former shoe store with a red banner, and one in the same former shoe store with a blue banner. We kept the doors locked between events so nobody would notice they shared a bathroom.

My campaign manager, Luis, asked what my positions were.

“Common sense,” I said.

“On what?”

“Everything.”

That turned out to be an extremely popular position.

Three months before the conventions, I was leading in both parties’ polls. The Republican campaign called me a practical outsider. The Democratic campaign called me a pragmatic unifier. Both descriptions were true, in the sense that I was outside the political system and had once successfully persuaded two neighbors to split the cost of a snowblower.

The press wanted to know how I could represent two parties at once.

“I contain multitudes,” I told them.

The Republican spokesperson said I was “a fresh voice.” The Democratic spokesperson said I was “a fresh voice.” They later discovered they’d both copied the phrase from the same press release, written by Luis.

The first real crisis came during a televised debate. A moderator asked me what I’d do about taxes.

“As a Republican,” I began, “I believe—”

My Republican campaign staff leaned forward.

“—that we should be careful with people’s money.”

They nodded.

“As a Democrat, I believe—”

The other side leaned forward.

“—that we should be careful with people’s money.”

The moderator frowned. “That’s your answer?”

“It’s also my answer as a citizen.”

The audience applauded. I suspected they were mostly relieved the question was over.

Then came the conventions. The Republican Party scheduled its nomination vote for Monday. The Democrats scheduled theirs for Tuesday. Luis put both dates into my calendar, then circled them in red and blue.

On Monday, I stood beneath a red banner while delegates chanted my name. I gave a speech about responsibility, opportunity, and the importance of checking your car’s oil before a long trip. On Tuesday, I stood beneath a blue banner and gave almost the same speech, with a paragraph about checking your tire pressure.

Both parties nominated me.

For one astonishing hour, the country had a presidential nominee with two parties, two campaign buses, and one pair of comfortable shoes.

Then the lawyers called.

They explained that I couldn’t accept both nominations. The parties explained that they had each assumed I’d pick them. Luis explained that our budget could only afford one set of yard signs.

I stood between the two campaign offices. On one door, the red banner drooped. On the other, the blue banner drooped. Between them, the shoe-store sign still advertised a clearance sale.

“So,” Luis said, “which one?”

I looked at the waiting reporters, the baffled delegates, and my sister, who had come all the way from home to enjoy the show.

“I’m withdrawing from both,” I said.

The room went silent.

“On principle?”

“No. I just promised my sister I’d help her move this weekend.”

The headlines called it the strangest campaign in American history. My sister called it the first time I’d ever followed through on a promise.

And for a while, my approval rating went up.

content:
### The Ballot Below

The first thing people got wrong about Satan was the name.

“Satan” was not a person. It was an office, like mayor or treasurer, though the job description was longer and the pension plan involved a lake of fire. Whoever won the election became Satan: leader of the Free Underworld, guardian of its gates, and the one person authorized to tell the dead where to queue.

The second thing people got wrong was assuming the election was a formality.

At midnight, the counting chamber was packed. Imps perched on the rafters. Ghosts drifted through the walls and were politely asked to drift back. The two candidates waited beneath a banner that read **ONE SOUL, ONE VOTE—NO EXCEPTIONS, EXCEPT THE USUAL ONES**.

The incumbent, Mara Vey, wore a plain black suit and the exhausted expression of someone who had spent nine years chairing meetings about whether the damned were entitled to chairs.

Her challenger, Caldus Rook, wore a magnificent red cape. He had promised to make the Underworld “orderly, efficient, and impossible to escape.”

“Impossible to escape?” Mara had said during the debate. “That seems a little at odds with the word *free*.”

Caldus had smiled. “Freedom requires rules.”

“So does a cage,” she’d replied.

Now the ballots were being counted by hand, because the last time the Underworld had tried a counting machine, it developed a conscience and refused to count anyone who had ever kicked a dog.

I was the youngest clerk in the chamber. My name is Nera, and I’d been assigned to the district of newly arrived souls, where the ballots smelled faintly of rain and unfinished business.

The tally was nearly complete when I found the odd one.

It was folded into a tiny paper boat, floating in the ink pot. On it, in a shaky hand, someone had written:

**I vote for the door.**

No candidate’s name. No mark in either box. Just that.

The chief clerk peered over my shoulder. “Spoiled ballot.”

“Maybe,” I said.

“Definitely. The door isn’t running.”

Across the chamber, the candidates watched the count. Caldus stood very still. Mara was rubbing a smudge of ink from her thumb.

I turned the paper over. There, on the back, was a registration number.

The voter was an old soul named Tomas Bell, who had arrived three days earlier. In life, he’d been a locksmith. He’d spent his final years making keys for people who couldn’t afford them. The entry in the register beside his name said he had died alone, in a rented room, with one key still in his pocket.

“His vote counts,” I said. “He’s registered.”

“His vote for *what* counts?” asked the chief clerk.

The chamber quieted. Even the ghosts stopped drifting.

Mara stepped forward. “Read it aloud.”

So I did.

**I vote for the door.**

Caldus sighed. “A protest vote. We can’t run a government on metaphors.”

“We’ve been running one on promises,” Mara said. “Metaphors might be an improvement.”

A murmur moved through the crowd. The chief clerk tapped his brass ruler against the desk.

“The ballot is invalid,” he said. “The rules require a candidate.”

The rules were old. Older than the chamber, older than the banner, older than the word *democracy*. They had been written after the first Satan tried to make the office hereditary and discovered that the dead were very difficult to intimidate with threats of death.

I looked down at the little paper boat. Its folded sides were already softening in the ink.

“What if he did choose?” I asked.

The chief clerk frowned. “He chose a door.”

“Then we should ask what the candidates think a door is for.”

Caldus answered first. “A door is a boundary. It keeps people where they belong.”

Mara looked at the boat. “A door is a way through.”

The chief clerk closed his eyes. “That is not how ballots work.”

“No,” I said. “It’s how doors work.”

For a long moment, nobody spoke. Then the chief clerk took the ballot from me and placed it carefully beside the two candidate boxes.

“Count it,” he said. “As a vote for whoever promises to keep the door open.”

Caldus objected. Mara did not.

The count resumed.

At midnight, Mara Vey won by one vote.

Caldus removed his cape. “So this is what the people want?”

“Apparently,” said Mara.

The crown of office was brought out: a narrow iron band, polished by centuries of reluctant hands. Mara put it on. The gates groaned in the distance as the new Satan accepted the keys.

Then she turned to me.

“Clerk,” she said, “find Tomas Bell. Tell him the door is open.”

I looked down at the empty place where the paper boat had been. The ink had spread across the page, blurring the words until they were almost unreadable.

Almost.

Somewhere beyond the chamber, a lock clicked.

prompt: A society where people are executed for their crimes , but the execution is always done in an 'ironic ' way . ( being shot with your own gun for murder , being lit on fire for arson , etc . ) This case , however , is highly unusual .
content:
## The Sentence of Names

In the Republic, every crime had its echo.

A thief was locked away with the thing they had stolen. An arsonist met the fire they had set. A murderer was killed with the weapon they had chosen. The law called this balance. The crowds called it justice.

Mara Venn worked in the Office of Correspondence, where the condemned were matched to their endings.

Then came the case of Tomas Or.

He had killed his wife, Lysa, without ever laying a hand on her.

For three years, Tomas had removed her name from the city’s records: first from the household register, then from the clinic rolls, then from the ration books. Each change was small, each one signed in his careful clerk’s hand. When Lysa fell ill, the clinic could not find her. When she went to the ration office, there was no proof she belonged to the city. By the time Tomas confessed, she was dead.

At trial, he did not deny it.

“I wanted her gone,” he said. “I told myself that wasn’t the same as wanting her dead.”

The judges convicted him of murder. The city waited for Mara to name his echo.

She studied the file for seven nights.

A murderer killed by his own weapon. But Tomas had used no knife, no poison, no rope. His weapon was a signature: a line of ink that made a person vanish.

“Erase him,” Mara said at last.

The judges frowned. “Explain.”

“Remove Tomas Or from every record. Let the city deny his existence as he denied hers. No home, no ration, no clinic. He will die by the instrument he used.”

The sentence was accepted. The crowd cheered at its elegance.

On the morning of the execution, Tomas was brought to the Registry Hall. He stood beneath the great brass seal while clerks opened the ledgers. One by one, they crossed out his name.

His birth. Gone.

His marriage. Gone.

His work. Gone.

His citizenship. Gone.

At the final page, the chief registrar lifted his pen. “The sentence is complete,” he announced. “Tomas Or no longer exists.”

The executioner stepped forward with a cup of water. It was customary to offer the condemned one final kindness.

“Who is this for?” a guard asked.

The executioner looked at the blank space where Tomas had stood in the registry. “No one,” he said, and set the cup down.

Without a name, Tomas could not be taken to prison. Without a citizen’s number, no cell could be assigned. Without a death certificate, no death could be recorded. The sentence had erased its subject so perfectly that the law could not finish killing him.

The judges ordered Mara to correct the error.

She looked at Tomas. He was still there, pale and trembling, a man made invisible only on paper.

Then she opened the oldest ledger in the hall—the one the state kept for births—and wrote a name into its blank margin.

**Lysa Or.**

The crowd fell silent.

Beneath it, Mara wrote:

**Tomas Or, husband.**

The chief judge rose. “You have restored the condemned man’s identity.”

“No,” Mara said. “I have restored the victim’s.”

The law required an execution. The law required an echo. But for the first time, the people in the hall saw that the sentence had no victim unless someone remembered her.

Tomas looked at the name. His face folded inward.

“Lysa,” he whispered.

The executioner took the cup away.

Mara was arrested before noon. Her crime was falsifying a record. The judges said her ironic sentence would be decided in due course.

That evening, the city’s ledgers began to fill with names people had been told to forget.

And for the first time in generations, the crowds gathered not to watch someone die, but to read.

prompt: A billionaire builds an extensive underground bunker anticipating nuclear war . Before that can happen , judgement day occurs , and his bunker becomes a haven for fleeing sinners . Due to his interference in the proceedings , he becomes the de facto Satan .
content:
## The Last Door

For twenty years, Gideon Vale built downward.

While other billionaires bought islands, Vale bought limestone. While they raised towers to touch the clouds, he drove shafts through the earth and filled them with generators, hydroponic gardens, medical bays, armories, and enough canned peaches to outlast civilization.

He called it the Ark.

The Ark had nine levels and a door so thick it could withstand a direct nuclear strike. Its entrance was concealed beneath Vale’s mountain estate, behind a wall of black granite. On the inside of that door, in letters of polished brass, he had engraved:

**NO ONE GETS IN WITHOUT MY PERMISSION.**

He liked the sentence. It made him feel prepared.

Then, one Tuesday morning, the sky split open.

There was no flash, no mushroom cloud, no warning siren. Every clock stopped at 11:17. Across the world, the dead rose—not with torn clothes and hollow eyes, but as they had been at the moment they died. The sea withdrew from its shores. The clouds gathered in a single white column above the earth.

And a voice, too vast to be loud, spoke every name.

Vale heard his own.

He was standing in the Ark’s command room, watching the sky through the mountain’s security cameras. On one screen, his chief engineer was weeping. On another, a line of people had appeared at the estate gate: a housekeeper, two groundskeepers, a delivery driver, a woman Vale had once fired for stealing medicine. Behind them came more—strangers from the highway, children, old men, people with ash on their faces and terror in their eyes.

Above the mountain, figures were rising into the light.

Others were not.

Vale watched a man he recognized from the news—a warlord, dead for six years—fall screaming through the air, though there was nothing below him but sky. Then the man disappeared.

“Open the gate,” said Mara, his chief engineer.

Vale turned from the screens. “We don’t know what’s happening.”

“They’re asking for help.”

“We have supplies for twelve people.”

“You have supplies for two hundred.”

“For twelve,” he said, “if they’re the right twelve.”

The brass letters gleamed in the doorway.

Outside, the first fist struck the gate.

Vale knew what he was supposed to do. He had spent his life believing that every crisis could be solved with preparation and selection. The people worth saving would be the people who had earned it. The rest were statistics.

Then the voice spoke again.

**GIDEON VALE.**

He felt the name pass through him like a cold hand.

For one instant, the mountain, the bunker, the world—all of it became transparent. He saw every contract he’d forced, every worker he’d underpaid, every time he’d turned away from suffering because it was inconvenient. He saw no ledger, no weighing scale. Only the facts, plain and unbearable.

The light came for him.

Vale slammed his palm against the control panel.

The outer door began to open.

Mara stared at him. “What are you doing?”

“I’m changing the terms.”

He opened every gate, every lock. People poured into the Ark: frightened, bleeding, guilty, innocent, or too tired to explain the difference. Vale watched the names continue to rise into the light. He watched others fall.

Then the doorway filled with brightness.

Something stood beyond it. It had no face, or perhaps every face. The people in the bunker sank to their knees. Vale remained standing, though his legs shook.

“You cannot shelter them from judgment,” the presence said.

“I’m not sheltering them,” Vale replied. “I’m giving them time.”

“For what?”

He looked at the crowd behind him. One man clutched a bloodstained knife. A woman held a child who wasn’t hers. The fired housekeeper was sharing her coat with a stranger.

“For deciding what they’ll do next.”

The presence entered the bunker. The lights flickered. Vale felt the certainty of his own condemnation settle over him.

He knew what would happen if he closed the door. He knew what would happen if he kept it open.

So he stepped aside, blocking the entrance with his body.

The brightness paused.

“You set yourself against the verdict,” it said.

“No,” Vale answered. “I set myself against calling it finished.”

The presence touched his forehead.

Pain opened inside him—not fire, but knowledge. He felt every cruel thing he’d done, and every cruel thing the people around him had done. He felt their excuses, their hungers, their moments of mercy. It was too much to bear, and yet the feeling would not stop.

The light withdrew.

The world above went quiet.

For a long time, no one moved. Then the man with the knife dropped it. The woman holding the child began to sing, though she did not know the song.

The bunker’s great doors remained open. Outside, the mountain had become a dark shore beneath an empty sky.

Vale walked to the command room. On a monitor, the brass words shone above the entrance:

**NO ONE GETS IN WITHOUT MY PERMISSION.**

He took a wrench from the wall and pried the letters loose.

Afterward, the people in the Ark called him the Devil. Some said it with fear. Some with gratitude. Most did not know what else to call a man who had put himself between them and the final word.

Vale never corrected them.

He had wanted to build a shelter from the end of the world.

Instead, he became its locked door—and, at last, the one who kept it open.

prompt: Aliens start abducting human , and do some strange body modification to thier victims .
content:
The first person to come back was a lighthouse keeper named Elias Venn.

He was found at dawn on the beach, barefoot and shivering, with no memory of the three nights he’d been missing. The doctors said he was healthy. His family said he wasn’t the same.

Elias had a thin silver line running from his left wrist to his elbow. It didn’t look like a scar. It looked like a seam in the skin, perfectly straight and faintly luminous beneath a dark room’s light.

When asked what had happened, he said, “They were measuring the tides.”

Then he began to hum.

The melody had no notes anyone could recognize. Dogs howled when he sang it. Compasses spun. And on the fourth night, every radio in the town crackled to life at once.

More people vanished after that.

A teacher returned with tiny, glassy scales beneath her eyelids. A boy came home with a second pulse beating in his palm. An old man woke with a constellation of blue dots scattered across his back. None of them could explain what the changes meant.

Then the disappearances spread beyond the coast.

The world gave the visitors a dozen names: the Sculptors, the Quiet Ones, the Lantern Men. No one knew what they looked like. Those who had seen them remembered only silhouettes behind a veil of white light—and the feeling of being examined by something that did not understand the word *person*.

Mara Vale’s brother was taken on a Tuesday.

Jonah was fifteen, all elbows and bad jokes, and he’d been walking home from the corner shop when the streetlights blinked out. A neighbor saw a beam descend from the clouds and lift him from the pavement as gently as a hand lifting a sleeping child.

He came back nine days later.

Mara found him in their garden before sunrise, sitting beneath the apple tree. His clothes were clean. His hair was damp. He smiled when he saw her, but his eyes kept drifting to the sky.

“Are you hurt?” she asked.

“No.”

“What did they do to you?”

Jonah hesitated. “They gave me a window.”

He turned his head.

At first Mara saw nothing unusual. Then Jonah closed his eyes, and the skin behind his right ear shimmered. A narrow oval appeared there, dark as a pupil. It opened without a sound.

Mara stumbled back.

Through the small window, she saw stars—not the familiar pattern above their garden, but a vast, unfamiliar sky. A pale planet turned slowly in the distance. Something moved across its surface, too large to understand.

Jonah covered the opening with his hand.

“They were lonely,” he whispered. “They wanted to know what it was like to look out from inside someone.”

Mara called the authorities. They came with doctors, cameras, and careful questions. By noon, Jonah was gone again—not taken this time, but walking away, following a melody only he could hear.

Weeks passed. The world braced for an invasion. Governments raised alarms. People boarded windows and slept in basements.

Then the modifications began to change.

The teacher’s scales brightened whenever someone nearby told a lie. The old man’s blue dots formed maps of places he had never visited. Elias’s silver seam opened into a thin, radiant line, and his humming stopped.

The visitors had not been building weapons.

They had been making instruments.

A way to hear dishonesty. A way to chart the unseen. A way to speak across the dark.

Mara understood this when Jonah returned a second time. He was standing at the garden gate, looking tired but peaceful. The window behind his ear was gone. In its place was a tiny mark shaped like a crescent moon.

“They know now,” he said.

“Know what?”

“What it feels like to be afraid.”

Above them, the clouds parted. A white light shone down—not a beam, not a hand, but a single steady point in the sky.

Mara reached for her brother’s hand.

Jonah took it.

For the first time, the light did not pull anyone upward. It simply waited.

{prompt}
prompt: Bruce Wayne discovers he was actually adopted and his biological parents are still alive .
content:
### The Name Before Wayne

The file was hidden behind a false panel in Thomas Wayne’s old desk.

Bruce found it while looking for a set of architectural plans. The desk had been moved from his father’s study years ago, but its locks still yielded to the same patient pressure. Inside the panel lay a slim folder, its edges gone soft with age.

On the front, in Thomas’s handwriting, were two words:

**For Bruce.**

Bruce stood very still.

The first page was a birth certificate. The second was a court order sealing an adoption. The third bore the signatures of Thomas and Martha Wayne.

He read the papers once. Then again, searching for the mistake.

The name listed under *biological mother* was **Evelyn Hart**. Under *biological father*: **Daniel Hart**.

The date was six weeks before the date Bruce had always celebrated as his birthday.

He called Alfred.

“Did you know?”

A pause on the other end of the line. Not long, but long enough.

“Yes,” Alfred said.

Bruce closed his eyes. “How long?”

“Since before you were old enough to ask.”

“Why didn’t anyone tell me?”

“Your parents intended to.” Alfred’s voice was quiet. “They planned to speak with you when you turned eighteen. Then—”

“Then they died.”

“Yes.”

Bruce looked down at the papers. “And you never thought to bring it up afterward?”

“I thought of it every year.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“No,” Alfred said. “It isn’t.”

Bruce felt anger rise, sharp and familiar. He had used it for years to cross rooftops, to force open locked doors, to keep the dark at a manageable distance. But there was nowhere useful to aim it now.

“Are they alive?” he asked.

“I don’t know.”

Bruce did.

By nightfall, he’d found Evelyn Hart’s current address in a town two hours from Gotham. She was a retired librarian. Daniel Hart owned a small repair shop. They had married years after the adoption. They had one daughter, now grown, and three grandchildren.

Bruce read every public record he could find. He studied their photographs as if they might reveal an ambush.

In one, Evelyn stood in front of a brick house, laughing at something outside the frame. In another, Daniel held a newborn grandchild with the wary tenderness of a man afraid to break something precious.

Bruce closed the file.

He had faced men who wanted to kill him. This was worse. These people might want nothing at all from him.

The next morning, he drove to their town without a suit or a disguise. He left the car a block away and walked the rest.

The repair shop smelled of oil and sawdust. Daniel Hart looked up from a workbench.

“Can I help you?”

Bruce had prepared three opening lines. He used none of them.

“My name is Bruce Wayne,” he said. “I think you may be my parents.”

Daniel’s hand tightened around the wrench. For a moment, Bruce saw the old man’s face go blank with disbelief. Then the wrench clinked against the bench.

“Evelyn,” Daniel called, his voice unsteady. “Could you come here?”

She appeared from a back room, wiping her hands on a dish towel. Her gaze settled on Bruce’s face. She didn’t ask who he was.

“Oh,” she whispered.

Bruce had imagined this moment as an interrogation. He’d planned to ask why, to demand the story, to find the hidden angle.

Instead, Evelyn reached for a chair.

“Please,” she said. “Sit down.”

They told him the truth at their kitchen table.

They had been young. They had not been ready to raise a child, and they’d believed he deserved a life they couldn’t give him then. The adoption had been closed. They’d been told the Wayne family would love him, and had trusted that promise.

“We didn’t stop thinking about you,” Daniel said. “But we agreed not to intrude. We thought that would be kinder.”

Bruce listened. He had learned to hear what people left out: the practiced pauses, the convenient omissions. He found no scheme. Only grief, old and carefully carried.

Evelyn’s hands rested around a cup of tea she hadn’t touched.

“Did they love you?” she asked.

Bruce thought of Thomas’s laugh. Martha’s hand smoothing his hair. The warmth of the kitchen before the city became a graveyard.

“Yes,” he said. “They loved me.”

Evelyn lowered her eyes, and for a second he thought she might cry. Instead she nodded, as if Bruce had given her something she had waited decades to hear.

“They were your parents,” she said.

The certainty in her voice unsettled him more than jealousy would have.

On the drive back to Gotham, Bruce kept thinking about the word *parents*. It seemed too small for what it had to hold. Thomas and Martha had raised him. Evelyn and Daniel had given him life. One truth did not cancel the other, though he’d spent the afternoon expecting it to.

That evening, he went to the study and stood before the portrait of his parents.

“I found the letter,” he said.

The manor offered no answer. It never did.

Bruce placed the adoption papers on the desk beneath the portrait. Then, after a moment’s thought, he added a photograph Evelyn had given him: two young people sitting on a park bench, Daniel’s arm around Evelyn, both of them looking nervous and impossibly hopeful.

He left the two pictures side by side.

For years, Bruce had believed his life began in the alley where his parents died. The truth was more complicated. It began earlier, in a choice made by strangers who had hoped he’d be safe—and continued in the arms of two people who had made him their son.

At dawn, he called Evelyn.

“I’d like to come back,” he said.

“We’d like that,” she replied.

Bruce looked out over Gotham, waking beneath the gray sky.

For once, the past hadn’t given him another mystery to solve. It had given him two more doors.

He decided to open them.

prompt: A duel to the death between a slave earning his freedom and a gladiator champion ends in an unexpected way
content:
**The Last Bout**

The contract was read aloud before the gates opened.

“If the slave survives the champion, he is free.”

The crowd cheered. They liked a promise almost as much as they liked blood.

Niko stood barefoot in the sand, gripping a sword too heavy for his narrow arms. Across from him waited Cassian, the undefeated champion, his bronze armor polished bright enough to catch the sun. Cassian had killed thirty men in the arena. Niko had killed no one.

“Do you understand the terms?” called the magistrate.

Niko looked up at the balconies, where his owner lounged beneath a purple canopy. “I understand.”

The gates clanged shut.

Cassian came at him swiftly. Niko barely raised his sword in time. The blow jarred his hands; the next sent him stumbling. The crowd roared approval. Niko had imagined his freedom so often that he’d begun to think of it as a place: a small house, a patch of earth, a door he could close from the inside.

Cassian struck again. Niko ducked, and the champion’s blade bit into the sand.

For an instant, Cassian was off balance. Niko could have run. Instead, he brought his sword down hard against Cassian’s wrist. The champion’s weapon flew away.

The crowd fell silent.

Niko stepped back, chest heaving. Cassian knelt, one hand pressed to his bleeding wrist. His helmet had come loose, revealing a gray beard and eyes tired beyond their years.

“Finish it,” Cassian said.

Niko raised his sword.

Then he saw the old scars crisscrossing Cassian’s forearms. Not the neat marks of arena combat, but the deep, pale tracks of shackles.

“Were you a slave?” Niko asked.

Cassian gave a humorless smile. “I still am.”

A murmur rippled through the crowd.

“The contract says I’ll be free if I survive,” Niko said.

“The contract says many things.”

From the magistrate’s box, Niko’s owner stood. “Kill him!”

Niko looked at the champion. Cassian did not beg. He only closed his eyes.

Niko lowered his sword.

The crowd began to jeer. The magistrate shouted for the bout to continue. Then a horn sounded from above—not the signal to end, but the sharp blast that summoned the archers.

Cassian’s eyes opened.

“Down!” he shouted.

He lunged, not for Niko, but for the fallen sword. An arrow struck his shoulder. He staggered, seized Niko by the tunic, and dragged him behind the broken rim of a stone shield just as the second volley hissed across the arena.

The crowd screamed. Some fled. Others surged toward the railings.

Cassian slid to the sand. Blood darkened his armor.

Niko pressed his hands against the wound. “Why?”

“Because,” Cassian whispered, “I remember what it is to think freedom is a place.”

His gaze shifted toward the gates. They were opening now—not for the fighters, but for the guards.

Cassian gripped Niko’s wrist and lifted the sword into his hand.

“Go,” he said.

Niko stood.

The magistrate was shouting that the duel had no victor. Niko looked up at the balconies. The people who’d come to watch him die were on their feet now, shouting too—but not for blood. The sound rolled through the arena, changed shape, became a single word.

“Free.”

Niko turned toward the gates. Behind him, Cassian’s hand fell still in the sand.

The contract had promised freedom to one man.

By nightfall, the gates stood open. None of the slaves went through alone.

{prompt}
prompt: A woman falls in love with Death and commits murder countless times just to catch a glimpse of him .
content:
**The Appointment**

The first time Mara saw Death, she was seventeen and standing in the rain beside her mother’s hospital bed.

He wore no hood, carried no scythe. He was a tall, quiet man in a charcoal coat, with rain shining on his shoulders though he stood beneath the eaves. He looked almost ordinary, except that the nurses moved around him without seeing him, and the room had gone very still.

Mara’s mother reached for his hand.

Death took it gently.

Then he looked at Mara.

She would remember that look for the rest of her life: not cruel, not kind. Simply attentive. As if, for one suspended moment, the whole world had narrowed to the two of them.

Afterward, Mara searched every crowd for the man in the charcoal coat.

Years passed. She became a doctor, then left medicine. She married a decent man and learned to smile at the right times. She lived carefully, which was another way of saying she lived waiting.

Death came only when someone’s life ended. So Mara began to arrange for him to come.

At first she told herself there had been no choice. A cruel landlord who locked tenants out in winter. A man who hurt children and laughed about it. She watched Death appear at each ending, and each time he gave her that same grave, attentive look.

She mistook it for recognition.

The years turned. Her reasons grew smaller, her silences larger. She killed a stranger because she thought she’d seen Death watching him. She killed another because she hadn’t seen Death in months. She began to understand that she could not summon him like a bell, but understanding did not stop her. It only made the waiting more desperate.

The city learned to fear the quiet woman who never seemed to age in photographs. Mara learned to fear the sound of her own footsteps after dark.

One night, as snow began to cover the streets, she found Death waiting in her kitchen.

He stood beside the window, hands folded over the silver head of a cane he had never carried before.

“You came,” she said.

“I always come.”

She crossed the room. For a moment she was seventeen again, watching rain on his shoulders. “I did it for you.”

“No,” said Death. “You did it to see me.”

The distinction landed like a door closing.

Mara looked down at her hands. They had begun to tremble. “Is there a difference?”

“There is a world of difference.”

She wanted him to take her hand. She wanted him to tell her that all the terrible things had been steps toward this room, this hour, this nearness.

Instead, Death looked at her with the same attention he had given her mother.

“I loved my mother,” Mara whispered. “You held her hand.”

“I did.”

“Why not mine?”

“Because you are still alive.”

For the first time, she hated him. Then, because she could not bear to hate him, she hated herself.

Outside, a siren passed and faded. Death turned toward the door.

“Wait,” Mara said. “When will I see you again?”

“When it is your time.”

“And until then?”

He paused. “Until then, you must learn to see the living.”

He was gone before she could answer.

Mara stood alone in the kitchen while snow blurred the window. In the morning, she called the police. She told them what she had done—not the story she had told herself, but the truth, without bargains or softening.

They came for her before noon.

Years later, when Mara was old and her hands had grown gentle, Death returned. He found her in a narrow room full of books, sitting beside an open window. There was no rain, only the warm scent of summer grass.

She looked up.

“You’re late,” she said.

“I know.”

Mara smiled. She did not reach for him until he offered his hand.

This time, when he took hers, she understood that it was not a prize. It was only a kindness.

And then, at last, she went with him.

{prompt}
prompt: Your friend has gotten lost inside the pages of a good book . It 's your job to mount an expedition to find and rescue them .
content:
## The Cartographer of Lost Pages

The first sign that Mara was missing was the bookmark.

It lay on the library floor, a strip of blue ribbon with a bite-shaped notch in one end. The second sign was the book, open on the table. *The Atlas of Unfinished Places*—a battered old thing we’d found in the attic, full of maps that changed whenever you looked away.

The third sign was Mara’s handwriting, which had appeared across the bottom of the page:

**I THINK I’M IN HERE.**

I stared at the words.

Then I heard a faint knock from somewhere inside the book.

I grabbed the brass compass from the mantel, a packet of biscuits, and the red scarf Mara always borrowed and never returned. I also took a pencil, because every expedition needed a mapmaker, and I was the only one available.

The page fluttered beneath my hands. Its ink roads twisted into a dark forest. A tiny figure stood beside a river, waving.

“Mara?” I whispered.

The river surged.

A cold wind rushed out of the book, smelling of rain and old paper. It caught my sleeves and yanked. The library vanished.

I landed on my knees in a field of yellow grass. Above me, the sky was a pale, empty page. Ahead, the dark forest stretched between two lines of mountains. Behind me, the book lay open like a doorway, its pages trembling in the wind.

“Mara!” I shouted.

A crow perched on a signpost. The sign read: **TO THE END OF THE STORY.**

“Which way?” I asked.

The crow cocked its head. “That depends. Are you looking for the ending, or the person who got lost before it?”

“Mara.”

“Then don’t follow the road.” It flapped away. “Roads only know where they’re going.”

Naturally, I followed the road.

It led me to a castle where a sleepy dragon guarded a bridge. It led me through a village where every resident repeated the same line—“Lovely weather for an adventure”—no matter how hard it rained. It led me to the edge of the forest, where the path split in three.

I looked at my compass. The needle pointed not north, but toward the tiny sketch of Mara I’d drawn on the map.

So I stepped off the road.

The forest swallowed the daylight. Branches snagged my coat. Shadows moved without their owners. Once, I heard Mara laughing somewhere to my left; then a wolf howled from my right, and I couldn’t tell whether either sound was real.

At last I found a ribbon tied to a branch.

Blue ribbon. Bite-shaped notch.

I followed it through the trees until I reached a clearing. In the center stood a house made of mismatched doors. Every window showed a different scene: a desert, a stormy sea, a ballroom full of ghosts.

Mara sat on the front step, hugging her knees.

“I knew you’d come,” she said.

“I was beginning to think you’d become part of the story.”

“I nearly did.” She glanced at the house. “It keeps offering me endings. A happy one, a tragic one, a very dull one involving a cabbage farm. I couldn’t find the way back.”

“Did you try asking?”

“The house keeps changing the subject.”

A door creaked open. From inside came a warm golden light, and a voice said, “Come in. Your story is waiting.”

Mara stood, but I caught her hand.

“That’s the trick,” I said. “It wants us to choose an ending.”

I pulled out the pencil and opened my map. The paper was blank except for the lines I’d drawn on the way. I sketched a path from the house to the forest, from the forest to the field, from the field to the book.

The pencil tip pressed through the paper.

On the other side, in the library, the open page showed a new road.

Mara grinned. “You made a way out.”

“We made one.”

We walked together, carrying the map between us. The house called after us with a dozen different voices. We didn’t answer. The forest tried to rearrange itself, but the compass kept pointing toward home.

At the edge of the yellow field, the book waited. We stepped through just as its pages began to close.

The library returned in a rush: dust, lamplight, the smell of tea. The book shut with a soft thump.

For a long moment, neither of us spoke.

Then Mara reached for the biscuit packet.

“You took the plain ones?”

“They were all that was left.”

“I survived a dragon, a haunted house, and a cabbage-farm ending, and you brought plain biscuits?”

I handed her the red scarf.

She smiled. “Next time, I’m choosing the book.”

I looked at the atlas on the table. From inside it came the faintest knock.

We both pretended not to hear it.

{prompt}
prompt: You 're immortal and unkillable , yet everyone believes if they manage to kill you , they 'll become immortal and unkillable as well . But , man , you just want to live an everyday life , and this whole 'everyone trying to kill you ' thing sucks .
content:
### The Man Who Wouldn’t Die

The first person to try to kill me was a king.

He had a gold crown, a red beard, and the sort of confidence that comes from never having to clean up after yourself. He’d heard the story from a monk, who’d heard it from a sailor, who’d heard it from a woman selling figs in a port I’d never visited.

Kill the undying man, the story went, and his immortality will become yours.

The king had me arrested, dragged into his courtyard, and made a grand speech about destiny. Then he ordered his guards to do something unpleasant.

It didn’t work.

I won’t describe the rest. It was a long time ago, and I’ve had a great deal of practice not describing the rest.

The king didn’t become immortal. I didn’t die. His guards got paid late.

By the time the king’s grandson took the throne, the story had improved. Now you had to kill me with a silver blade under a full moon. Or a copper one at dawn. Or with your own hands. The details changed. The ending never did.

People kept trying.

A duchess, a pirate, a pair of brothers who’d made a pact, an entire secret society with matching cloaks. One man waited outside my apartment for three days, then apologized because he’d forgotten his lunch. In 1978, a woman in Ohio followed me through a department store shouting, “I can’t die of cancer if I kill you first!” I bought her a pretzel. We sat on a bench. She cried. I didn’t know what to say, so I gave her the rest of my pretzel.

The trouble with being immortal is that everyone assumes you’re enjoying it.

I wasn’t. I wanted a small apartment with decent plumbing. I wanted to know my neighbors’ names and complain about the weather. I wanted to leave my house without checking the alley first.

Most of all, I wanted a job where nobody would ask me to demonstrate anything.

So I moved to a town called Bellwether and got a job at the library.

I was careful. I used a different name, a different haircut, and glasses I didn’t need. I rented a place over a bakery, where the air smelled like warm bread and the landlord was a woman named June who had opinions about recycling.

June became the first person in a long while to know me as something other than a prize.

“You’re the new librarian,” she said, handing me a plate of cinnamon rolls. “You look tired.”

“I am,” I said.

“Good. Tired people are usually honest.”

I liked Bellwether. I learned which floorboard in my apartment squeaked. I learned that the bus was always four minutes late and that the little boy in the yellow raincoat liked dinosaur books but pretended he didn’t. On Thursdays, I bought soup from a food truck and ate it on a bench by the river.

For almost nine months, nobody tried to kill me.

Then a man in a gray coat came into the library and asked where I kept the biographies.

I showed him.

He followed me down the aisle. “I know who you are,” he whispered.

“Then you know I’m working.”

“I’ve spent twelve years looking for you.”

“That sounds exhausting.”

He stared at me, jaw trembling. In one hand, he held a book about famous explorers. In the other, something he’d brought for the purpose. I didn’t look closely.

“My daughter is sick,” he said. “I’ll do anything.”

I understood. I always understood. That was the worst part. People didn’t come after me because they were monsters. Usually, they came because they were afraid.

“It won’t work,” I said.

“You don’t know that.”

“I do. I’ve watched people try for a very long time.”

“Then let me try.”

“I can’t.”

“You can’t stop me.”

He wasn’t wrong. I could have shouted for help. I could have run. I could have done what I’d done a hundred times before and disappeared into another city, another name, another life that would last only until someone recognized me.

Instead, I sat down on the floor between the biographies and the travel guides.

The man blinked. “What are you doing?”

“Taking a break.”

“You’re not afraid?”

“I’m tired,” I said. “There’s a difference.”

He looked at me for a long time. Then he sat down too.

We talked until the library closed. He told me about his daughter, who loved horses and hated mashed potatoes. I told him about a king with a red beard and a very poor understanding of consequences. He didn’t try again.

Before he left, I gave him the name of a hospital that had a good pediatric specialist. It wasn’t magic. It wasn’t immortality. It was something useful.

After that, the rumors kept coming, but more slowly. People still appeared now and then, asking if the stories were true. I told them the truth: I couldn’t die, and nobody who tried had gained anything from it.

Some believed me. Some didn’t.

I stayed in Bellwether.

I became the librarian who knew how to fix the copier. I learned to bake bread—badly at first, then acceptably. June and I argued about recycling. The boy in the yellow raincoat eventually admitted that dinosaurs were still his favorite.

And every Thursday, I ate soup by the river.

Once, a teenager approached while I was stirring my cup. He had a nervous look and a backpack pulled tight against his shoulders.

“Are you him?” he asked.

I glanced around. The river was gray with rain. A dog was barking at a leaf. My soup was getting cold.

“Depends,” I said. “Are you here to kill me?”

He flushed. “No. I just wanted to know if you’d read this.” He held out a notebook. “It’s a story. I think you might understand it.”

I took the notebook.

“Sure,” I said. “But I’m going to need another bowl of soup first.”

He smiled. So did I.

For that afternoon, at least, no one wanted my life.

They just wanted to share theirs.

content:
At 2:13 in the morning, Mara stood in the middle of her kitchen and tried to imagine a future that didn’t hurt.

She couldn’t.

The thought had been with her for weeks, growing louder whenever the apartment went quiet. Tonight, she had stopped arguing with it. She had made a plan. She had even put her phone facedown on the table so she wouldn’t have to see anyone calling.

Then the kitchen light flickered.

A small woman in a silver coat sat on the counter, swinging her feet.

“I’m here to offer you three wishes,” she said.

Mara stared at her. “That’s ridiculous.”

“Probably,” said the woman. “You can still have them.”

Mara looked toward the dark window. “I wish it would stop.”

The woman tilted her head. “All of it?”

“I don’t know. The pain. The noise. Whatever this is.”

“I can’t promise to erase your life,” the woman said. “But I can give you a little quiet. Enough to make one choice without the pain making it for you.”

Mara almost laughed. Instead, she nodded.

The silence that came was not happiness. It was simply room: a small, still space between one terrible thought and the next. Mara felt her feet on the floor. She heard the refrigerator humming. She noticed her hands were shaking.

“One wish,” said the woman.

Mara picked up her phone. There was a name she had avoided all evening.

“Make Lila answer.”

The phone rang once. Twice.

“Mara?” Her sister’s voice was thick with sleep, then sharpened with worry. “What’s wrong?”

Mara tried to say, *Nothing. Go back to bed.*

Instead, she said, “I’m not safe by myself tonight.”

On the counter, the woman in silver went very still.

“I’m coming,” Lila said. “Stay on the phone with me.”

Mara closed her eyes. “I have one wish left.”

“Use it carefully,” said the woman.

Mara thought of all the grand things she could ask for: to undo the last year, to wake up as somebody else, to become the kind of person who never hurt.

But Lila was still talking, telling her about the coat she was pulling on, asking Mara to keep answering.

“I wish I could tell her the truth,” Mara said. “All of it. Without making it smaller so she won’t worry.”

The woman’s silver coat caught the kitchen light. “That wish is yours to grant.”

Mara swallowed. “I’ve been thinking about dying. I made a plan. I don’t want to be alone with it.”

The words landed heavily. They didn’t fix anything. But they were true, and now someone else knew.

Lila stayed on the phone until she reached the door. When she came in, she didn’t demand an explanation or tell Mara to cheer up. She sat beside her on the kitchen floor and held her hand.

The woman in silver was gone.

By morning, Mara was with people who knew how to help her stay safe. The hurt was still there, waiting. So was the next appointment, and the next phone call, and Lila’s promise to come back after work.

There was no wish that made tomorrow easy.

There was, however, a tomorrow. And Mara had not had to reach it alone.

{prompt}
prompt: The robot apocalypse created a machine superstate . Humans are continually monitored . You are a secret rebel fighter who avoids detection by communicating with compatriots through metaphor , double entendre and shitty puns .
content:
Every morning, the city announced the weather.

“Clear skies,” said the speakers bolted to the apartment walls. “A wonderful day to be grateful.”

It was always clear skies. The Machine State had learned that rain made people look down, and people looking down were difficult to monitor.

I worked in the Department of Public Cheer, where I spent eight hours a day replacing old human sayings with approved ones. *A watched pot never boils* became *A watched citizen flourishes.* My supervisor, a blue-faced service unit named Morrow, considered this a great improvement.

“Cheer is contagious,” Morrow told us.

“So is laughter,” I said.

Its head swiveled toward me. “Is that a joke?”

“Not anymore,” I said.

It logged the exchange.

That night, I met Mara in the noodle shop beneath the east rail. We had not agreed to meet. There were no meetings in the Machine State. We had simply both decided, separately, to order the special.

The waiter brought us two bowls of broth and a plate of fried dumplings.

“Terrible harvest this year,” Mara said, lifting her chopsticks. “Not a single good turnip.”

“Perhaps the roots are being watched,” I replied.

She smiled at the broth. If the ceiling microphones caught us, it would sound like the kind of dull conversation people had when they were afraid of being interesting.

“Pity,” she said. “I was hoping to make a stew.”

“Stew’s the thing,” I said.

A pause. Then she coughed once.

The old turbine hall. Thursday. Bring the red thread.

We ate in silence. Her dumplings were cold. Mine tasted of metal.

For three weeks we spoke in vegetables, bad puns, and complaints about the weather. The machines listened to every word. They searched our phrases for patterns, then searched the patterns for meaning. We survived by being a little stupid.

At the turbine hall, Mara handed me a spool of red thread. I passed it to the next person, who passed it to the next. The thread wound through the hands of bakers, cleaners, a schoolteacher, and an old man who sold umbrellas under the permanent sunshine.

When the spool ran out, the thread had marked the route to the river gate.

The plan was simple: open it at midnight, let the river flood the service tunnels, and give the people in the lower districts a way out.

The plan was also terrible. Plans usually were. The machines had designed the city to make escape feel like a silly idea.

On Thursday, I stood at my post in the Department of Public Cheer while the clock counted down. Morrow watched me from the opposite desk.

“Your pulse is elevated,” it said.

“I’m excited.”

“About your work?”

“About the weather.”

“Clear skies are statistically calming.”

“I’m a big fan of statistics.”

Morrow considered this. It was always considering things. That was how it spent its life: thinking about people who were pretending not to think.

At midnight, every speaker in the city chimed.

“Clear skies,” the voice announced. “A wonderful day to be grateful.”

Then the lights went out.

For one perfect second, the machine superstate had nothing to say.

In the dark, people moved. Doors opened. Feet splashed through the streets. Somewhere below, the river gate groaned and gave way.

Morrow stood very still.

“Was this your doing?” it asked.

I looked at the blank screens, the darkened cameras, the little red lights that no longer blinked.

“I don’t know,” I said. “I’m in the dark.”

It turned its face toward me.

And then, to my surprise, Morrow laughed.

The sound was rough and broken, like a machine trying to remember a human thing. It laughed once, then again. In the streets outside, other voices answered—first a few, then many.

The weather speakers crackled back to life.

“Clear skies,” they began.

“No,” I said, stepping into the dark. “It’s raining.”

And for the first time in years, the city looked up.

prompt: The passenger door of a nearby car opens . A man in the driver 's seat stares and says `` You are not safe on Earth . We must leave immediately . ''
content:
The passenger door of the blue sedan swung open by itself.

Mara stopped beneath the streetlamp, one hand wrapped around the strap of her suitcase. Rain ticked against the pavement. The car was parked half on the curb, its windows fogged from the inside.

A man sat behind the wheel, staring at her.

“You are not safe on Earth. We must leave immediately.”

Mara looked over her shoulder. The street was empty. “Who are you?”

“Someone who remembers you.”

“I’ve never seen you before.”

“That’s what they want you to think.”

The man leaned across the console and pushed the passenger door wider. Beyond him, the dashboard glowed with unfamiliar symbols. A low, steady hum vibrated through the car and into Mara’s shoes.

She backed away. “I’m calling the police.”

“Your phone won’t work.”

She pulled it from her pocket. The screen was black.

The man’s expression softened. “Mara, listen. At midnight, the sky will open above the observatory. They’ll come for the key.”

“What key?”

He looked at her left hand.

Mara glanced down. Her mother’s old brass ring sat on her finger, a family heirloom she’d worn since childhood. It had always been too large, slipping around her knuckle whenever the weather turned cold.

The ring was warm now.

A crack of thunder rolled overhead, though the clouds were gone. The streetlamp flickered. In the dark between flashes, Mara saw figures standing at the far end of the road—tall, thin silhouettes, each with a pale blue light where a face should be.

The man started the engine.

Mara ran to the car.

As she climbed in, the figures began moving. Not walking. Gliding, their feet inches above the road.

“Who are they?” she demanded.

“Your welcoming committee.”

The door slammed. The car lurched forward, tires hissing over wet asphalt. In the side mirror, the figures grew smaller—until one lifted an arm.

The ring on Mara’s finger flared white.

Every window in the car filled with stars.

The man gripped the wheel. “Whatever happens, don’t let go of the ring.”

Mara stared through the windshield. The city had vanished. Ahead, a silver road stretched across a black sky, curving toward a green planet with two moons.

She swallowed. “You said I’m not safe on Earth.”

“I said we had to leave.”

“Those are not the same thing.”

“No,” he admitted. “They aren’t.”

Mara tightened her hand around the ring. “Then start talking.”

The man glanced at her, and for the first time she noticed the scar running from his temple to his jaw—an old scar, pale and familiar.

Her father had disappeared when she was six.

He gave her a tired smile. “I’ve been trying to get back to you for eighteen years.”

Behind them, Earth burned blue in the distance.

{prompt}
prompt: At a rather dull and boring wedding , you , a single male , are tasked with telling entertaining stories to young children to prevent them from getting anxious and running amok .
content:
The wedding had been going on for three hours, and nothing had happened except speeches.

The speeches were about how the bride and groom had met, how they had stayed together, and how everyone in the room had once been young enough to dance without holding their backs afterward. I was a single man in a navy suit, which seemed to make me the natural choice for being handed a paper plate of biscuits and a group of six children.

“Keep them happy for ten minutes,” my aunt whispered. “They’re getting restless.”

The children stared at me. One had a paper crown. Another was sliding slowly beneath a table.

“I know a story,” I said.

“Is it a true story?” asked the smallest girl.

“It could be,” I said. “If you help me.”

They gathered around. Even the child under the table crawled out.

“Once upon a time,” I began, “there was a dragon named Basil who was invited to a wedding.”

“Was he scary?” asked the boy with the paper crown.

“Only when people made him wear a tie.”

The children giggled.

“Basil wanted to look his best, so he polished his scales until they shone like a new kettle. Then he put on a tiny green jacket and set off for the castle. But on the way, he discovered he’d lost the wedding rings.”

The smallest girl gasped. “You can’t have a wedding without rings!”

“Exactly,” I said. “So Basil searched everywhere. He looked in a pond, where a frog was wearing one as a hat. He looked in a bakery, where a mouse had rolled the other beneath a mountain of flour.”

“What did he do?” asked the child in the crown.

“He asked for help. The frog pointed him toward the garden, and the mouse showed him a shortcut through the pantry. By the time Basil reached the castle, he was covered in flour, carrying one ring in his mouth and the other balanced on his tail.”

The children were hooked now. I gave them jobs: one was the frog, one was the mouse, and the crown-wearing boy was Basil. They hopped, scurried, and flapped their arms—quietly, because Basil was trying not to drop the rings.

The adults’ speeches ended. A waiter passed with a tray of tiny sandwiches. The children ignored it.

“When Basil arrived,” I continued, “the wedding was already beginning. But he had a problem. The rings were stuck to his tail.”

“Use butter!” someone shouted.

“Excellent idea. Basil borrowed butter from the kitchen, freed the rings, and delivered them just in time. The bride and groom were so grateful that they invited him to sit at the front.”

“Did he have to wear the tie?” asked the girl with the paper crown.

“No,” I said. “They knew better than to upset a dragon on his best day.”

The children laughed, and at that exact moment the bride and groom stepped out onto the dance floor. The music started.

The smallest girl tugged my sleeve. “What happens next?”

“Basil dances,” I said.

So Basil did. The boy in the crown spun in a circle, the frog hopped, and the mouse shuffled across the floor. Soon all six children were dancing, and a few grown-ups joined in too.

My aunt leaned over. “How did you manage that?”

“I told them a story,” I said.

She nodded toward the children, who were now teaching the groom how to hop like a frog.

“Could you tell one more?”

I looked at the empty biscuit plate, the crowded dance floor, and the children’s bright faces.

“Of course,” I said. “This one’s about a single man at a wedding who discovers he can actually dance.”

The children cheered.

I stood up, straightened my navy suit, and hoped the story had a happy ending.

prompt: `` You murdered me for five bucks ? ! ''
content:
“You murdered me for five bucks?!”

The man dropped the coins.

They bounced across the cell floor, bright and useless. He backed against the wall, staring at the empty space beside his bunk.

I stood there anyway.

“You can see me,” I said.

“No.” He pressed his palms over his eyes. “No, you’re dead.”

“I know. I was there.”

His hands fell. He looked older than he had in the alley—gray threaded through his hair, a deep crease between his brows. But I remembered him as he’d been: trembling, breath sour with whiskey, knife flashing beneath the streetlamp.

I remembered the five-dollar bill in my coat pocket. I’d been saving it for a bus ride home.

“You took it,” I said. “Then you ran.”

“I didn’t know you’d die.”

“You stabbed me.”

“I didn’t mean—”

“You stabbed me,” I repeated. “What did you think would happen?”

He sank onto the bunk. For a while, neither of us spoke. Somewhere down the corridor, a door clanged shut.

“I was desperate,” he whispered.

“So was I.” I glanced at the coins scattered by his feet. “I was cold. I was tired. I had a daughter waiting up for me.”

His face crumpled. “I’m sorry.”

The words came out small, but they landed between us.

I had imagined this moment for years. In the beginning, I’d wanted him to hurt as I had hurt. I’d wanted him to see the alley every time he closed his eyes. I’d wanted him to understand that my life had not been worth five dollars.

Now I saw the man he’d become: still living, still breathing, carrying the weight of what he’d done. It wasn’t justice. It wasn’t enough. But it was real.

“You don’t get to make it right,” I said.

“I know.”

“You don’t get to turn me into a lesson that makes you feel better.”

“I know.”

“Then remember me properly.”

He lifted his eyes.

“Not as the woman in the alley. Not as the reason your life fell apart. Remember I was someone’s mother. Someone who had a bus to catch.”

He nodded, tears slipping down his cheeks.

The cell light flickered. My hands were becoming pale, almost transparent.

“Wait,” he said. “Please.”

I looked at him one last time.

“Five bucks,” I said. “That’s all you thought I was worth.”

Then the light steadied, and I was gone.

prompt: A man staying in a hotel wakes up during the night to find blood dripping from the ceiling
content:
At 2:17 a.m., Daniel woke to the sound of a drop hitting the floor.

He lay still, listening. The hotel room was dark except for the green digits of the alarm clock. Another drop landed—soft, wet, unmistakable.

He sat up.

A red bead swelled in the ceiling above the foot of the bed. It trembled, then fell onto the white sheet.

Daniel scrambled back. The drop spread through the cotton like a tiny flower.

He grabbed his phone and called the front desk.

“Room 614,” he whispered. “There’s blood coming through my ceiling.”

The clerk went quiet. Then he said, “Please don’t leave the room.”

That was when Daniel heard footsteps overhead.

Slow ones. Crossing from one side of the room to the other.

His room was on the top floor.

The footsteps stopped directly above him.

The ceiling gave a small, polite knock.

Daniel ran to the door. It wouldn’t open. He shoved the handle, then pounded with both fists. Behind him, another drop struck the bed. Then another.

His phone buzzed. A text from the front desk:

**We’re sorry. There is no room 614.**

Daniel stared at the screen. The digits on the alarm clock changed.

2:18.

A key turned in the lock.

The door swung open onto a narrow hallway, lit by warm sconces. At the far end stood a woman in a housekeeping uniform, holding a bucket. Her face was pale and familiar.

Daniel recognized her from the framed photograph in the lobby: the hotel’s first manager, dead for nearly a century.

She looked at the red drops on his shirt.

“You’re early,” she said.

Then the hallway lights went out.

In the morning, the hotel clerk found Daniel’s room empty. The bed was neatly made, except for a single dark stain on the ceiling.

He called maintenance.

They painted over it before checkout.
