content:
## Errata

The first rule I ever broke was written in gold above the courthouse doors:

**A creature may take one action on its turn.**

It sounded simple. It wasn’t.

I was twelve, and my mother was being evicted. The bailiff had a key. I had a broom, two cousins, and a very literal understanding of the word *creature*. We took turns using the Help action to distract him while my youngest cousin picked the lock.

The courthouse doors opened. Mother stayed.

By morning, the rule had been amended. **A creature may take one action on its turn. The Help action does not grant advantage on an attempt to open a lock unless the helper is proficient with thieves’ tools.**

My cousins and I were famous for a week.

After that, I made a living finding the lines the world hadn’t thought to write.

People called me a loopholer. The Crown called me a nuisance. The gods, who maintained the rules, called me nothing at all. They simply issued patches.

The patches appeared at dawn, in shining letters across the sky.

**ERRATA 3.08: A creature cannot benefit from the same spell more than once per round.**

**ERRATA 4.12: Falling damage is capped at twenty dice.**

**ERRATA 5.01: A locked chest is not a creature.**

I kept a book of them. I made a note whenever a patch closed one door and left another ajar.

Then the river came down.

It tore through the east quarter while half the city slept. Roofs became rafts. Rafts became kindling. By sunrise, the temple steps were crowded with the injured, and the healers had run out of spell slots.

My sister Mara was among them. She had a broken leg, a split scalp, and a talent for making bad situations sound like jokes.

“Don’t look so miserable,” she told me. “You look like you’re about to try something.”

“I am.”

“That’s what I’m afraid of.”

I had one ninth-level spell left: *Wish*. In the old days, people used it to make palaces, or enemies disappear, or themselves into kings. I had spent years reading the spell’s fine print.

It could duplicate any spell of eighth level or lower without requiring the usual components.

And a *simulacrum* was a spell of seventh level.

I wished for a copy of myself.

The world made one out of snow and moonlight. It had my face, my memories, my voice. It also had all the spells I had prepared that morning.

The copy looked at the wreckage, looked at me, and said, “Well. That seems useful.”

It used *Mass Cure Wounds* on the temple steps.

Then it used *Wish* to make another copy of itself.

The next copy healed the next group. The one after that made two more. By noon, the temple courtyard was full of me—some limping, some laughing, all of us kneeling beside the wounded.

We didn’t save everyone. No loophole can do that. But we saved Mara. We saved the baker’s twins. We saved a hundred people who would have died before the last healer’s rest was over.

For three days, the city called me a hero.

On the fourth morning, the sky filled with gold.

**ERRATA 11.04: A simulacrum cannot create another simulacrum. A simulacrum cannot regain expended spell slots.**

The copies stayed. The rule didn’t unmake them. It only stopped the chain.

They spent the next week helping where they could, then grew quiet as their magic ran out. One of them—June, who had my crooked smile and none of my patience—sat with Mara while her leg mended.

“You know,” June said, “I thought being you would be more exciting.”

“It usually is,” I told her.

“Maybe that’s the problem.”

After the patch, people were angry. Some blamed me for making the gods notice. Others blamed the gods for waiting until after the flood to fix a spell that had been written for centuries.

I blamed myself, which was easier than choosing between them.

Then the Crown offered me a position in the Office of Arcane Compliance. They wanted me to find loopholes before anyone else did.

I took the job.

A month later, the Office announced a new regulation: copies made by magic were not to be considered citizens. The language was precise. The consequences were not.

I found a flaw in the wording before lunch. By supper, June and the others had signed their own petition.

We won them the right to keep their names.

The patch came three weeks later.

That is how the cycle works. Someone finds a gap. Someone uses it. Someone gets hurt, or saved, or rich. The gods close the gap. The closure leaves a seam. Someone else finds it.

People ask if I ever get tired of it.

I tell them yes.

Then I read the new rules.

Last night, a boy came to my office with a question about the wording in the latest patch. He was nervous, holding his hat in both hands. He wanted to know if he could show me something he’d noticed.

I looked at the sky, where tomorrow’s errata had not yet appeared.

“Go on,” I said. “Show me.”

prompt: I have no face .
content:
### The Shape of a Name

I have no face.

Not a hidden face, or a scarred one, or one I keep covered. My head ends in smooth skin, like a stone worn by water. No eyes. No nose. No mouth.

I can still see, breathe, and speak. No one knows how. They stop asking after a while.

When I was young, my mother taught me to recognize people by their footsteps. My father taught me their voices. At the train station, where I work now, I know the regulars by the way they say *good morning*. Mr. Vale whistles before he reaches the ticket window. The twins argue in perfect unison. Mrs. Osei hums when she’s worried.

I know thousands of people.

They know me as the person behind the glass.

One snowy evening, a little girl appeared at my window. She couldn’t have been more than six. Her coat was open, one mitten missing. She set a red wooden horse on the counter.

“I lost my mum,” she said.

I called the station guard. He asked what her mother looked like.

The girl shook her head. “I don’t know. She was wearing a blue scarf.”

The guard sighed and started asking around. But the girl leaned close to the glass.

“She sings,” she whispered. “When she thinks nobody can hear.”

“What song?”

The girl hummed four small notes, then stopped. She didn’t know the rest.

I did.

Every Thursday, a woman bought a ticket to Northbridge and sang those same four notes while she waited. She always stood at the far end of the platform, where the draft lifted her blue scarf. I had never seen her face. I had only heard her song.

I called the platform. The train was already pulling in.

The girl clutched her wooden horse. “Will you come with me?”

I came around the counter. People stared as I took her hand. They always do, at first.

We hurried through the station, following the little tune she hummed. On the platform, a woman was searching beneath the benches, her blue scarf trailing in the wind.

The girl let go of my hand and ran.

Her mother gathered her up, sobbing into her hair. Then she looked at me.

“Oh,” she said. “You found her.”

I nodded.

The woman’s eyes moved over the smooth blankness of my face. I knew the moment she reached the question people always reached.

Instead, she said, “Thank you.”

Then she began to sing.

The girl joined in, clumsy and loud. I walked back to my window alone, listening until the train carried their voices away.

I have no face.

But now, when that woman comes to the station, she calls me by my name.
